title: LinkedIn Open to Work: The Real Trade-Off Between the Green Banner and Recruiters-Only
h1: LinkedIn Open to Work: What the Green Banner Reveals and What Recruiters-Only Actually Hides
seo_title: LinkedIn Open to Work: Banner vs. Recruiters-Only Explained
seo_description: LinkedIn open to work has two settings, not one. See what your current employer can see, and which setting fits your situation before you turn it on.
excerpt: LinkedIn's Open to Work feature isn't one switch, it's two different settings with very different visibility to your current employer. Here's what each one actually shows, who should use which, and where LinkedIn's own privacy promise has limits.
content_html:
Turning on LinkedIn open to work means choosing between two different settings, not one feature. The public option adds a green #OpenToWork frame around your profile photo that every visitor to your profile can see, including colleagues and your current manager. The private option, sometimes called "recruiters only," shares your job-seeking status with people using LinkedIn Recruiter without adding any visible frame to your photo. LinkedIn says it takes steps to hide the private version from recruiters at your current employer and closely related companies, but its own guidance stops short of guaranteeing that — which is the trade-off almost every guide to this feature skips over.

The two settings, and what each one actually does

The public #OpenToWork banner

This is the green photo frame you've likely seen on LinkedIn. It's visible to everyone: your connections, recruiters, hiring managers browsing your profile, and anyone at your current company who looks you up. LinkedIn also lets you add up to five target job titles and preferences (remote, hybrid, on-site; job type; start date) that show in a card below your headline.

The private "recruiters only" setting

This shares the same information — job titles, preferences, availability — but only with LinkedIn members using the paid LinkedIn Recruiter product. There's no visible badge on your profile for regular connections or visitors. It's the version built for people who are employed and job hunting quietly.

Who can see itPublic bannerRecruiters-only setting
Your 1st-degree connectionsYes, visible on your photo everywhereNo visible badge
2nd/3rd-degree connections and strangersYesNo
Recruiters using LinkedIn Recruiter, unrelated companiesYesYes
Recruiters at your current employerYes, fully visibleLinkedIn attempts to hide it, but doesn't guarantee it
Third-party agency recruiters staffed on your employer's accountYesPossible edge case where hiding may not apply
Effect on recruiter outreachHigher visibility, more InMail volumeLower visibility, only reaches Recruiter-seat users

What your current employer can and cannot see

This is the part worth getting exactly right before you turn anything on. If you use the public banner, your current employer — anyone at your company, whether they recruit or not — can see it the moment they view your profile, the same as any other visitor. There's no special hiding logic for the public setting; it's genuinely public.

The recruiters-only setting is designed specifically to solve this problem, but the mechanism behind it is matching, not a hard block. LinkedIn tries to detect your current employer from your profile's work history and hide your open-to-work status from recruiters associated with that same company or its listed affiliates. That matching can miss two common cases: a third-party staffing agency or contract recruiter working on behalf of your employer without being formally listed as the same company, or a subsidiary or sister company that isn't linked in LinkedIn's company data the way you'd expect. In both cases, someone effectively recruiting for your employer could still see your status, even though you selected the private setting specifically to avoid that.

Practically, this means: if your company is small enough that internal recruiting is done directly by an in-house talent team clearly tagged under your employer's LinkedIn company page, the recruiters-only setting works close to as advertised. If your company uses external staffing vendors or has a complex group structure — common with larger Indian conglomerates and IT services firms — treat the "cannot guarantee 100% privacy" line as a real caveat, not boilerplate.

The real trade-off: visibility vs. risk

The public banner exists because it measurably increases recruiter outreach. Career blog The Interview Guys, citing internal engagement data, reports that profiles with the public Open to Work frame get meaningfully higher response rates from recruiter InMails than profiles without any signal — the site cites figures around 14.5% response versus roughly 4.6% for profiles with no visible signal. That's a real incentive for anyone actively searching without a current job to protect.

The downside shows up differently depending on your situation:

  • If you're unemployed or a final-year student: the public banner has almost no downside. There's no current employer to alert, and the visibility boost works in your favour, particularly during placement season when volume of applications matters.
  • If you're currently employed and searching quietly: the public banner is the wrong tool. Your manager or HR seeing the green frame on your own company's LinkedIn feed is a common, avoidable way people accidentally announce a job search before they're ready to.
  • For senior or leadership roles: some recruiters read the public banner as a signal of lower demand — that you're seeking opportunities rather than being sought after — which can work against you in a way it usually doesn't for freshers or early-career roles where actively signalling interest is expected and normal.

How to turn it on (and choose the right setting)

  1. Go to your LinkedIn profile and click "Open to" below your headline, or click the pencil/edit icon next to your profile photo.
  2. Select "Finding a new job."
  3. Add up to five job titles you're targeting, your location preferences, and job types (full-time, internship, contract).
  4. Choose visibility: "All LinkedIn members" (the public banner) or "Recruiters only" (the private setting).
  5. Save. If you chose the public option, the green frame appears around your profile photo within a few minutes.

You can switch between the two settings at any time, and turning it off entirely removes both the banner and the private signal immediately.

How this compares to Naukri's visibility settings

If you're job hunting across both LinkedIn and Naukri, the mental model is similar but not identical. Naukri's profile has a visibility toggle and an "actively looking" style status recruiters see when searching its database, and separately lets you hide your profile from specific companies, including your current employer, by name — a more direct block than LinkedIn's attempt-to-detect approach. If protecting your current job is the priority, using Naukri's named-company exclusion alongside LinkedIn's recruiters-only setting gives you two different mechanisms rather than relying on one imperfect one.

With LinkedIn's Indian user base past 200 million as of mid-2026 according to analytics tracker NapoleonCat, and companies at the scale of TCS, Infosys, and Wipro all running structured LinkedIn Recruiter searches for both fresher and lateral hiring, the platform's visibility settings aren't a minor detail — they determine who sees your job search before you're ready to tell them yourself.

What Open to Work does not do

It's worth being clear about what this feature is not, since a lot of confusion about it comes from assuming it does more than it does.

  • It does not apply to jobs automatically. Open to Work is a visibility signal, not an application. You still need to apply to postings or respond when a recruiter reaches out; the badge simply makes you easier to find and slightly more likely to get a first message.
  • It does not notify your connections when you turn it on. There's no broadcast post or notification blast telling your network you've flipped the setting — people only see it when they visit your profile or see your photo elsewhere on the platform, such as in comments or posts.
  • It does not guarantee recruiter outreach. The banner increases the odds of being contacted; it doesn't obligate any recruiter to reach out, and a weak profile behind the badge won't convert extra visibility into extra interviews.
  • It does not replace a tailored application. Recruiters browsing Open to Work profiles are still filtering by skills, location, and experience level in their search — an outdated headline or missing skills section means you may not surface in relevant searches even with the badge on.

What to check before you turn it on

Since the public banner draws more eyes to your profile, do a quick pass on the basics first: an updated headline that states the role you actually want (not your current job title by default — see these headline examples if you're stuck), a photo that's recent and professional, and a skills section that matches the job titles you've added to your Open to Work preferences. A badge pointing at an unfinished profile does more harm than good, since it's often the first thing a recruiter's eye lands on before reading anything else.

If your profile still needs broader work before you're ready for extra visibility, it's worth fixing that first rather than turning the banner on immediately — our guide on LinkedIn profile optimisation covers the headline, About section, and skills changes that matter most before you start actively signalling that you're looking.

Who should use which setting

Final-year students and freshers

Use the public banner. There's no current employer to protect, and the visibility boost helps during the highest-volume part of the year for campus and off-campus hiring. Pair it with a resume built around a proven resume format for freshers, since the banner brings more eyes to your profile, and a weak resume linked to it does more harm visible than invisible.

Employed professionals job hunting quietly

Use the recruiters-only setting, and treat the "cannot guarantee" caveat seriously if your company uses external recruiting vendors. Consider also reviewing who has visibility into your activity feed — liking or commenting on job posts publicly can be a bigger leak than the Open to Work setting itself.

Senior professionals and leadership candidates

Skip the public banner regardless of employment status; rely on direct outreach, a strong About section that states your track record clearly, and warm introductions instead, since the signalling effect at that level tends to work against you rather than for you. A mentor who has actually hired at that level can help you gauge whether a quiet approach or a visible one fits your specific market and function before you decide.

faq.q: Can my current employer see if I turn on LinkedIn Open to Work?
faq.a: It depends which setting you choose. The public #OpenToWork photo frame is visible to everyone, including your current employer. The private 'recruiters only' setting is designed to hide your status from recruiters at your current employer, but LinkedIn does not guarantee this works in every case, particularly if your employer uses third-party staffing agencies or has a complex company structure LinkedIn's matching doesn't fully capture.

faq.q: What's the difference between the green Open to Work banner and the recruiters-only setting?
faq.a: The green banner is public and visible to anyone who views your profile, including connections and colleagues. The recruiters-only setting shares the same job preferences privately, only with people using LinkedIn Recruiter, and adds no visible badge to your profile photo.

faq.q: Does the Open to Work banner actually help you get more recruiter messages?
faq.a: According to reporting from career site The Interview Guys, profiles with the public banner see meaningfully higher recruiter InMail response rates (cited at around 14.5%) compared to profiles without any signal (around 4.6%). The effect is strongest for early-career and mid-level roles; some recruiters read the banner differently for senior or leadership candidates.

faq.q: Should freshers use the public banner or the private setting?
faq.a: Freshers and final-year students with no current employer to protect generally benefit more from the public banner, since it increases visibility during high-volume hiring periods like campus placement season without any real downside.

faq.q: How do I turn on Open to Work on LinkedIn?
faq.a: Go to your profile, click 'Open to' below your headline or the edit icon on your photo, select 'Finding a new job,' add up to five target job titles and preferences, then choose either 'All LinkedIn members' (public banner) or 'Recruiters only' (private) before saving.

faq.q: Is there a way to hide my job search from my current employer more reliably than LinkedIn's setting?
faq.a: If you're also using Naukri, its profile settings let you block visibility to specific named companies, including your current employer, which is a more direct exclusion than LinkedIn's attempt to detect your employer automatically. Using both platforms' privacy tools together is more reliable than relying on either one alone.

title: BTech Fresher Resume Format: Complete Guide for India (2026)
h1: BTech Fresher Resume Format: A Complete Guide for Indian Students
seo_title: BTech Fresher Resume Format for India (2026 Guide)
seo_description: See the btech fresher resume format Indian recruiters check by branch, with a worked example and 2026 salary data by college tier. Build your resume today.
excerpt: The btech fresher resume format Indian recruiters actually check, broken down by branch — a full worked example, branch-specific skills, and 2026 salary data by college tier.
content_html:
The right btech fresher resume format is a single-page, single-column layout that leads with Education and CGPA, followed by a Skills section matched to your specific branch and target role, then Projects/Internships with measurable outcomes, because Indian recruiters across campus placement, off-campus drives, and Naukri applications screen fresher engineering resumes for branch relevance and CGPA cutoffs before reading anything else. What belongs in that Skills and Projects section differs enormously by branch and target function — a CSE fresher applying to a service company needs a very different resume from a mechanical fresher applying to a manufacturing plant, even though both are "B.Tech freshers." Below is the correct section order, a full worked example, and realistic 2026 salary data by branch and college tier, so you can calibrate expectations honestly rather than against inflated placement-brochure numbers.

Why "B.Tech Fresher" Isn't One Resume Template

The single biggest mistake in generic B.Tech resume advice is treating all branches the same way. A computer science fresher applying to Infosys, TCS, or a product company is judged almost entirely on projects, DSA fundamentals, and a couple of relevant technologies. A mechanical or civil fresher applying to a core manufacturing or construction firm is judged on CAD/site skills and CGPA cutoff, with almost no coding expectation at all. An electronics/ECE fresher sits somewhere between — some roles are software-adjacent (embedded, testing), others are hardware-and-core.

Before writing your resume, decide honestly which lane you're in: IT-services/product (most CSE/IT branches), core-technical (mechanical, civil, electrical hardware), or a hybrid (ECE, instrumentation). This piece covers the structure that works across all three, and flags where the content inside each section should diverge.

The Correct Section Order for Any B.Tech Fresher Resume

1. Header

Full name, phone, professional email (not a college nickname address), city, and LinkedIn URL. Skip the photo — most Indian ATS and recruiter screens don't need it, and some large-company portals actively discourage it.

2. Career Objective (optional, 2 lines)

Only include one if it names a specific target role and skill. "Seeking a challenging opportunity to utilise my skills" wastes the top of the page — either name the role and one real skill, or delete the section entirely and let Education/Skills speak for you.

3. Education

Degree, college, CGPA/percentage, and graduation year first, then Class XII and X with board and percentage. Many campus and off-campus drives filter by a CGPA cutoff (commonly 60% or 6.0-6.5 CGPA for IT-services mass hiring) before a human even opens the resume, so this needs to be visible immediately.

4. Technical Skills

Group by category and match your branch — programming languages and frameworks for CSE/IT, CAD/analysis tools for core branches, or a mix for ECE. Don't pad this with tools you've only watched a tutorial on.

5. Projects and Internships

This is where fresher resumes actually differentiate, since coursework is nearly identical across a batch. Two to three entries with a specific, measurable outcome each outperform five vague bullet points.

6. Certifications

NPTEL, Coursera, or relevant platform certifications, with issuing body and year — genuinely checked for technical roles, especially where they fill a gap your coursework doesn't cover.

7. Achievements and Extra-Curricular

Hackathons, technical fest wins, or leadership roles in student technical bodies — brief, at the end.

A Full Worked B.Tech Fresher Resume Example

This example is for a CSE/IT-track fresher applying to off-campus and Naukri drives; the same section order applies to core branches with the Skills and Projects content swapped for branch-relevant tools.

Priya Nair

Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu | +91-98XXXXXX63 | priya.nair@email.com | linkedin.com/in/priyanair | github.com/priyanair

Career Objective

B.Tech Computer Science graduate with hands-on experience in Java, SQL, and REST API development through two academic projects and a 3-month internship, seeking an entry-level software engineer role.

Education

B.Tech, Computer Science Engineering — PSG College of Technology | 2026 | CGPA: 8.1/10

Class XII (State Board) — 2022 | 88%

Class X (State Board) — 2020 | 91%

Technical Skills

  • Languages: Java, Python, SQL
  • Web/Backend: Spring Boot (basic), REST APIs, Node.js (coursework level)
  • Databases: MySQL, basic MongoDB
  • Tools: Git/GitHub, Postman, basic Docker
  • CS fundamentals: Data Structures & Algorithms (arrays, trees, graphs), DBMS, OS basics

Internship — Software Engineering Intern, [Mid-size IT Services Firm], Coimbatore (Feb–Apr 2025)

  • Built two REST API endpoints for an internal HR tool using Spring Boot, reducing a manual data-entry step for the HR team by automating a lookup that previously took 10 minutes per record
  • Fixed 14 bugs from the team's tracked backlog during the internship, all verified and merged after code review

Academic Project — Campus Lost-and-Found Portal (Final Year, 2025–26)

  • Built a full-stack web app (Java Spring Boot backend, MySQL, basic React frontend) used by 200+ students across two hostel blocks during a pilot run
  • Implemented a matching algorithm that auto-suggested likely matches between "lost" and "found" entries, cutting manual admin review time by an estimated 40% during the pilot

Certifications

  • NPTEL — Database Management Systems (2025)
  • Coursera — Java Programming and Software Engineering Fundamentals (2025)

Achievements

Finalist, [college name] 24-hour hackathon (2025) — built a working prototype for an attendance-automation tool as part of a 3-member team.

Skills and Priorities by Branch (What Recruiters Actually Check)

The table below is deliberately branch-specific, because "list your skills" means something different in each case.

BranchWhat gets screened firstCore skills/tools recruiters check
CSE / IT / AI-MLProjects, DSA fundamentals, CGPA cutoff (mass-hiring drives)A language (Java/Python/C++), SQL, basic system design or a framework, Git, DSA
MechanicalCGPA, internship/project depth, CAD proficiencySolidWorks/AutoCAD, GD&T, manufacturing process knowledge — see our mechanical engineer resume format guide
CivilCGPA, site exposure or design-software depth depending on trackAutoCAD, STAAD Pro, billing/site skills — see our civil engineer resume format guide
ElectricalCGPA, core-subject depth, PSU exam readinessMATLAB/Simulink, power systems basics, PLC exposure for industry-facing roles
ECEBranch-relevant projects; varies by IT-adjacent vs core targetEmbedded C, basic VLSI/digital design, or a software stack if targeting IT roles

What B.Tech Fresher Salaries Actually Look Like in India (2026)

Placement-brochure "average package" numbers are frequently inflated by a handful of outlier offers, so treat single-figure claims with caution. Findmycollege.com's 2026 salary-trends data, drawing on placement and salary-portal figures, shows fresher pay varying sharply by both college tier and branch: IITs and top NITs report average fresher packages of roughly ₹12-18 LPA, other NITs/IIITs/BITS-level institutes around ₹6-10 LPA, and tier-2/private colleges and state government colleges in the ₹3-6 LPA range. By branch, the same data shows CSE averaging ₹10-15 LPA, ECE around ₹7-12 LPA, IT around ₹6-10 LPA, electrical around ₹5-8 LPA, and mechanical and civil both around ₹4-7 LPA — a meaningfully lower band than the CS-adjacent branches, reflecting the core-engineering hiring market discussed in our mechanical and civil resume guides above.

College tierTypical fresher CTC (2026)
IITs / top NITs₹12–18 LPA (average; wide spread by branch and recruiter)
Other NITs, IIITs, BITS₹6–10 LPA
Tier-2 private engineering colleges₹3–6 LPA
State government colleges₹3–5 LPA

If you're at a tier-2 or tier-3 college, the honest reality is that most placement offers cluster at the mass-hiring end of the IT-services market (TCS, Infosys, Wipro-scale hiring) rather than the product-company end — that's not a reflection of your ability, it's the shape of the market, and it's worth planning off-campus applications around from day one rather than waiting on campus drives alone. See our guide on off-campus drives if your campus placement season is behind you or hasn't produced an offer yet.

Common Mistakes That Get B.Tech Fresher Resumes Rejected

One Generic Resume for Every Application

Sending the identical resume to a core-manufacturing walk-in and a software-services off-campus drive, with no adjustment to Skills or Objective, signals you haven't actually read the job posting.

Padding Skills With Tools You Can't Discuss

A long skills list with no project or internship behind most entries invites an interviewer to pick the weakest-sounding one and ask you to explain it — which usually goes badly if it's there purely for keyword coverage.

Burying CGPA or Education

Placing Education at the bottom of the page, after a long Objective and Skills section, delays the one data point most fresher-hiring filters check first.

No Measurable Outcome in Projects

"Developed a web application for student management" tells a recruiter nothing. Name the scale, the outcome, or the specific technical challenge solved, the way the worked example above does.

Getting the Resume Past Automated Screening

Large IT-services companies and many product companies run resumes through an ATS before a human sees them. Keep the layout single-column with standard section headings, and match the wording in your Skills section to the language of the specific job posting where it's genuinely accurate. For the mechanics of this, see how to pass ATS screening for the formatting rules that apply regardless of branch.

Off-Campus and Naukri Applications: What Changes

Once campus placement season ends without an offer, or if your college doesn't get strong drives for your branch, the resume itself doesn't need to change much — but your application volume and targeting strategy does. Off-campus and Naukri applications compete in a much larger pool with no CGPA-cutoff filter working in your favour the way a campus drive does, so the same resume needs to be paired with more precise targeting: apply to postings where your actual skills genuinely overlap with the listed requirements, rather than mass-applying to every "fresher" tag on the portal.

For CSE/IT-track freshers, this usually means widening beyond the big four IT-services companies to mid-size product companies, startups, and GCCs (global capability centres) that hire year-round rather than on a fixed placement calendar. For core-branch freshers, off-campus effectively means direct company career pages, walk-in drives at manufacturing clusters, and Naukri postings from Tier-1 suppliers and construction contractors, since these employers rarely run structured campus drives the way large IT firms do. In both cases, keep a tracking sheet of where you've applied and with which resume version, since you'll likely be running two or three tailored versions in parallel rather than one.

faq.q: What is the best btech fresher resume format for Indian job applications?
faq.a: A single-page, single-column layout with Education and CGPA near the top, a Technical Skills section matched to your specific branch and target role, then Projects/Internships with measurable outcomes, then Certifications and Achievements. The exact content of the Skills and Projects sections should differ sharply by branch — a CSE resume and a mechanical resume shouldn't look alike.

faq.q: Does a btech fresher resume need to be different for core branches versus CSE/IT?
faq.a: Yes, significantly. CSE/IT-track resumes are judged mainly on projects, DSA fundamentals, and relevant technologies, often screened through automated ATS parsing. Core branches like mechanical and civil are judged more on CGPA cutoffs, CAD/site skills, and internship depth, usually reviewed by a human at campus drives or walk-ins rather than an automated parser.

faq.q: What CGPA cutoff do Indian companies use for fresher hiring?
faq.a: Mass-hiring IT-services drives (TCS, Infosys, Wipro-scale hiring) commonly use a cutoff around 60% or 6.0-6.5 CGPA, though this varies by company and drive. Core-sector and product-company cutoffs vary more widely, so check the specific job posting rather than assuming a fixed number.

faq.q: What is a realistic B.Tech fresher salary in India by college tier?
faq.a: According to findmycollege.com's 2026 salary-trends data, IITs and top NITs report average fresher packages around ₹12-18 LPA, other NITs/IIITs/BITS around ₹6-10 LPA, and tier-2 private or state government colleges typically in the ₹3-6 LPA range. Branch matters too — CSE and ECE tend to sit higher than mechanical and civil.

faq.q: Should a B.Tech fresher have one resume or multiple versions?
faq.a: Multiple versions, tailored to the type of role. A generic resume sent unchanged to a core-manufacturing walk-in and a software off-campus drive signals you haven't read the posting. Keep the same section order, but adjust the Objective and Skills content to match the specific track.

faq.q: How many projects should a B.Tech fresher resume include?
faq.a: Two to three, each with a specific, measurable outcome, are more effective than five vague entries. Recruiters and interviewers use projects to differentiate fresher candidates whose coursework otherwise looks identical, so depth matters more than count.

title: How to Answer the Expected CTC Question Without Underselling Yourself
h1: How to Answer the Expected CTC Question in an Interview
seo_title: How to Answer the Expected CTC Question in Interviews
seo_description: Answer the expected CTC question with a range, not a number — and know when to defer. A practical script for freshers and 0-2 year candidates, with examples.
excerpt: A practical script for handling the expected CTC question in interviews, including what range to quote, when to defer, and how to avoid underselling yourself.
content_html:
The expected CTC question — "What are your salary expectations?" — shows up in almost every Indian interview, usually from HR, and most freshers either blurt out a number they haven't researched or undersell themselves out of nervousness. The right approach is to quote a researched range tied to the role and market, not a single figure, and to hold that range until you have a firm offer in front of you. This article gives you the actual wording to use, how to research the number beforehand using Naukri, Glassdoor and AmbitionBox, and how to handle the specific traps recruiters set — like being asked for your current CTC first, or being pushed for an exact figure on the spot.

Why This Question Trips Up Freshers Specifically

Experienced candidates usually have a current CTC to anchor from and a clear sense of market rate for their skill level. Freshers and people with 0–2 years of experience often don't — campus placement packages vary wildly by college tier, and off-campus offers vary even more, so there's no reliable personal benchmark to quote. That gap is exactly why an unprepared answer costs you money: quote too low and the company will happily pay you less than they budgeted; quote too high without justification and you risk getting screened out before a human even discusses it with you.

Research the Number Before the Interview, Not During It

Walking in without a number is worse than walking in with a slightly wrong one. Spend twenty minutes before the interview checking:

  • AmbitionBox and Glassdoor salary pages for the specific company and role — these are self-reported but useful for a ballpark, especially for large employers like TCS, Infosys, Wipro or Accenture where sample sizes are large.
  • Naukri's salary insights or recent job postings for the same role and experience band in your city, since compensation for the same title can differ by 30–40% between a metro and a tier-2 city.
  • Your own college's placement cell data or seniors who joined similar roles in the last one to two hiring cycles — this is often the most accurate signal for entry-level packages, more reliable than aggregator sites.

Once you have three or four data points, take the median, not the highest number you found — a single outlier posting skews your anchor and makes your ask look uninformed if the interviewer knows the real range.

What to Actually Say

Use a range, anchored slightly above the median you researched, and tie it explicitly to the role rather than a personal need.

"Based on my research for this role and experience level in [city], I'm looking at something in the ₹6–7.5 LPA range. I'm flexible depending on the full compensation structure and the role itself."

This works because it signals you've done homework, it gives the recruiter room to negotiate within a band you've already accepted, and it doesn't box you into a number you'll regret if the role turns out to include better benefits, a signing bonus, or faster growth than you expected. If you're asked to narrow it to one figure, give the midpoint of your range and stop talking — resist the urge to justify it further unless asked.

Handling the Specific Traps

"What is your current CTC?"

If you're a fresher with no prior CTC, say so plainly — there's nothing to hide. If you have a current job and don't want to anchor the new offer too closely to your old, low salary, you're allowed to keep the focus on the number you're seeking rather than disclosing the old one in detail: "My current compensation isn't directly comparable given the role and scope here, but I'm targeting ₹X–Y for this position." Several large employers still ask for payslips to verify current CTC during background checks, so don't misstate the number outright — keep the framing about the new role's scope, not the old figure's accuracy.

"Just give me one number."

If pushed, give the midpoint of your researched range and add one sentence of context: "If I had to pick one figure, I'd say ₹6.75 LPA, based on what similar roles at comparable companies are paying in this city." A single justified number beats a vague range delivered nervously.

"Can you take less because you're a fresher?"

This is a common pressure tactic, especially in off-campus drives and smaller companies. It's fine to hold your range if you've researched it properly — being a fresher doesn't mean your market value is arbitrary, it means your market value is at the entry-level band, which you should already have priced in.

What a Realistic Range Actually Looks Like by Experience Level

Ranges vary enormously by role, company tier and city, but here's a rough shape freshers and early-career candidates can use as a starting anchor before adjusting for their specific situation.

ProfileTypical CTC Range (Non-Metro)Typical CTC Range (Metro)
Fresher, mass IT recruiter (TCS/Infosys/Wipro-scale)₹3.5–4.5 LPA₹3.5–4.5 LPA
Fresher, product/startup, technical role₹4–7 LPA₹6–10 LPA
0–1 year experience, non-technical (ops, support)₹3–4.5 LPA₹4–5.5 LPA
1–2 years experience, technical role₹5–8 LPA₹7–12 LPA

These figures are directional, not guaranteed — always adjust against the specific company and role you're interviewing for using the research steps above, and check what portion is fixed vs variable, since a headline number with a large bonus or ESOP component isn't the same as an equal fixed CTC. Once you have an offer in hand, run the actual numbers through the in-hand salary calculator before comparing two offers, since take-home pay can differ meaningfully even at the same CTC depending on structure and city.

After the Number: What to Check Before You Accept

Getting the expected-CTC conversation right is only half the negotiation. Once an offer comes through:

  • Ask for the full CTC breakup, not just the headline figure — see our guide to salary slip components for what each line should represent.
  • Compare the offer against your current or previous CTC properly, not just the headline number, since the actual jump matters more in in-hand terms than CTC terms.
  • If there's room to push further, structure it as a specific ask tied to market data or a competing offer, rather than a general "can you do better" — see our broader guide on how to negotiate salary for the actual scripts.

What Not to Do

Don't quote a number you found once on a random forum and haven't cross-checked. Don't lowball yourself because you're worried about seeming greedy — recruiters expect a researched range, not a modest guess, and an unnaturally low number can even raise doubts about your confidence or self-assessment. And don't treat the first number you're offered as final if it's meaningfully below the range you researched and stated — a polite "I was expecting closer to my stated range given [specific reason]" is a normal part of the process, not a confrontation.

How Much of a Hike Is Reasonable When You're Switching Jobs?

If you're already employed and moving, recruiters and career forums frequently repeat a "20–40% hike" figure as the norm for a job switch. Treat that as a commonly repeated industry rule of thumb rather than a confirmed, sourced statistic — the real number depends heavily on how underpaid you currently are, the role's market rate, and how badly the new company wants you specifically. A more reliable way to set your own number is still the research method above: median market rate for the new role, compared honestly against your current CTC, not a flat percentage applied blindly.

If your current CTC is already below market rate

In this case, don't anchor your ask to a percentage hike over your current pay at all — anchor it to the market rate for the new role. If similar roles are paying ₹6 LPA and you're currently on ₹3.8 LPA, asking for "a 40% hike" undersells you; asking for something close to the ₹6 LPA market rate is the more defensible number, and you can say exactly that if asked to justify it.

If you're moving for a promotion in scope, not just a lateral move

A role with meaningfully more responsibility — say, moving from a support role to an analyst role, or from an individual contributor track to leading a small process — justifies a larger jump than a same-level lateral move. Frame this explicitly in your answer: "Given the scope of this role compared to my current one, I'm targeting ₹X, which reflects the added responsibility" reads as reasoned, not greedy.

What Recruiters Are Actually Assessing With This Question

HR isn't just collecting a number — they're also reading how you handle a slightly uncomfortable, high-stakes question. A candidate who freezes, gives a wildly unresearched figure, or immediately caves when pushed signals the same behaviour they'll likely show later when negotiating a raise, a project deadline, or a client conversation. Conversely, a calm, specific, well-justified range signals exactly the kind of preparation and self-advocacy that's genuinely useful on the job. Keep this in mind, because it also means how you say your range often matters as much as the number itself — steady pacing and a brief justification land better than a rushed, apologetic answer.

A Realistic Example Conversation

Here's roughly how this plays out for a fresher applying to a product company for a support/associate role, having researched a median of ₹4.8 LPA for the role in their city:

Recruiter: "What are your salary expectations?"

Candidate: "Based on what I've seen for this role and experience level in the market, I'm looking at somewhere in the ₹4.5–5.5 LPA range. I'm flexible depending on the complete structure — fixed versus variable, and any other benefits."

Recruiter: "Our budget for this role tops out at ₹4.2 LPA fixed, with a small variable component."

Candidate: "I appreciate you being upfront. Could you walk me through what the variable component typically pays out at, and whether there's a review point in the first year where this could be revisited?"

Notice the candidate doesn't immediately accept or immediately walk away — they ask a clarifying, specific follow-up that could still make the lower number acceptable, without sounding either desperate or difficult.

faq.q: How do I answer the expected CTC question with no work experience?
faq.a: State plainly that you're a fresher with no prior CTC to reference, then give a researched range based on similar roles at similar companies in your city — using AmbitionBox, Glassdoor, Naukri salary insights and your college placement cell's recent data. A range signals preparation better than a single guessed number.

faq.q: Should I give a range or a single number for expected CTC?
faq.a: Give a range anchored around the median of your research, slightly above it. A range gives the recruiter room to negotiate within a band you've already accepted, while a single number either anchors you too low or risks sounding arbitrary if you haven't justified it.

faq.q: What if the recruiter insists on one exact figure?
faq.a: Give the midpoint of your researched range and justify it in one sentence, referencing market data for the role and city. A justified single number is fine once you've been pushed for it; the mistake is leading with one before you've established your range.

faq.q: Is it okay to ask for more than my current CTC?
faq.a: Yes, and it's expected — career forums often repeat a 20-40% hike as the norm when switching jobs, but treat that as a commonly repeated industry rule of thumb rather than a confirmed statistic. What matters is that your ask is grounded in researched market data for the specific role, not an arbitrary percentage applied to your current pay.

faq.q: Can a company withdraw an offer if I quote a high expected CTC?
faq.a: A company can decide not to proceed if your expectation is far outside their budget for the role, but a well-researched, reasonably justified range rarely causes this on its own — most recruiters expect some negotiation. What does cause problems is refusing to engage with any range or being unable to justify the number when asked.

title: ATS Friendly Resume Template: 2 Formats You Can Copy Today
h1: ATS Friendly Resume Template for Indian Job Seekers
seo_title: ATS Friendly Resume Template for Indian Job Seekers
seo_description: See a ready ATS friendly resume template for freshers and 1-2 year professionals, built on rules Indian recruiters' ATS checks. Copy it now.
excerpt: Two complete, copy-usable ATS friendly resume templates — one for freshers, one for 1-2 years of experience — built around the formatting rules Indian ATS tools and recruiters actually check.
content_html:
An ATS friendly resume template is a single-column layout with plain section headings (Contact, Summary, Skills, Experience, Education, Projects), saved as a .docx file or a text-based PDF, that lets applicant tracking systems used by Indian recruiters — including Naukri's own parser, and enterprise systems like Workday and Darwinbox — read your name, dates, and skills correctly on the first pass. It avoids tables, text boxes, headers and footers, icons, and multi-column designs, because those are the exact layout choices that most often scramble parsing, according to Naukri's own resume-checker guidance. Below are two complete templates you can copy directly: one for a fresher with no full-time experience, and one for someone with 1-2 years on the job. Both follow formatting rules that Indian ATS tools and recruiters actually check, not generic "best practice" advice.

Why the Template Matters More Than the Design

Most Indian job seekers assume a rejected application means a recruiter looked at their resume and passed on it. Often, no human saw it at all. According to Jobscan's 2024 review of Fortune 500 job-application pages, 97.8% of large employers run a detectable applicant tracking system on every incoming resume, and the same category of parsing software sits behind Naukri, LinkedIn, and most company career portals used by high-volume recruiters like TCS, Infosys, and Wipro to sort thousands of applications for a single posting. The parser's only job is to convert your document into structured text — a name field, a dates field, a skills field, an experience-duration calculation. A template built around clean, linear formatting survives that conversion cleanly. A template built for visual impact — colour blocks, side columns, icon bullets, skill-rating graphics — frequently does not, and the recruiter never even sees the mismatch; they just see a candidate list where your name is missing or your skills are blank. For a deeper look at how the parsing itself works, see how ATS software works.

This is also why a template that looks impressive on a laptop screen can quietly fail before a human ever opens it. The fix is not to make your resume look plainer for its own sake — it is to separate two jobs that a resume has to do. The first job is surviving the parser: getting your name, phone number, dates, and skills extracted into the right fields without corruption. The second job is persuading a person once you are through. The templates below are built to pass the first test cleanly, and leave you free to focus your effort on writing strong content for the second.

The Non-Negotiable Formatting Rules

Before you even get to wording, the template has to obey a short list of rules. These come directly from Naukri's own published guidance for job seekers, and they line up with what every major ATS vendor's documentation says.

Fonts, File Type, and Naming

Use a standard font — Arial, Calibri, or Times New Roman — at 10-12pt body size. Save the file as .docx or PDF (a text-based PDF exported from Word, not a scanned image). Name the file FirstName_LastName_Resume rather than "Resume_Final_v3", since some systems display the filename to the recruiter.

Structure and Length

Keep the layout single-column, top to bottom, with no tables, text boxes, headers, footers, or graphics. A fresher resume should fit one page. Once you have 1-2 years of experience, a slightly fuller one page — or a page and a bit — is acceptable, but do not pad it to two full pages just to fill space.

ElementATS-safe choiceWhy it matters
LayoutSingle column, top to bottomTwo-column and table layouts are the single biggest cause of scrambled parsing
Contact detailsIn the body text, not a header/footerMany parsers skip header and footer regions entirely
File format.docx or text-based PDFScanned or image-based PDFs cannot be parsed into text at all
Section titlesStandard labels: Experience, Education, SkillsUnusual labels like "My Journey" are not recognised as section headers
BulletsSimple round or dash bulletsCustom icon bullets or symbols can render as blank or broken characters
DatesOne consistent format throughout (e.g. Jun 2023 – Present)Mixed date formats confuse experience-duration calculations

ATS Friendly Resume Template: Fresher (0 Experience)

This layout is built for a final-year student or recent graduate applying to campus placements, off-campus drives, or entry-level roles on Naukri. Copy the structure below and replace every bracketed placeholder.

Header

[Your Full Name]

[City, State] | [phone number] | [professional email] | linkedin.com/in/[yourname]

Summary

[Degree] graduate from [College Name] with hands-on experience in [core skill 1] and [core skill 2] through [number] academic/personal projects. Seeking an entry-level [target role, e.g. Software Engineer / Business Analyst] role to apply [specific skill] in a production environment.

Skills

  • [Technical skill 1], [Technical skill 2], [Technical skill 3]
  • [Tool/software 1], [Tool/software 2]
  • [Soft skill relevant to role, e.g. Client communication, Data analysis]

Education

[Degree Name, e.g. B.Tech in Computer Science] — [College Name], [City] | [Year of graduation] | CGPA: [X.X/10] or Percentage: [XX%]

[Class XII] — [School Name] | [Year] | [Percentage]

Projects

[Project Title] | [Tools/technologies used] | [Month, Year]

  • Built [what you built] to solve [specific problem], resulting in [measurable outcome or scope, e.g. "processed 500+ records" or "reduced manual steps by 3"]
  • Used [specific tool/technique] to [specific action taken]

[Second Project Title] | [Tools/technologies used] | [Month, Year]

  • [One or two lines describing scope and outcome, same structure as above]

Certifications and Achievements

  • [Certification name], [Issuing platform, e.g. Coursera/NPTEL], [Year]
  • [Relevant achievement, e.g. hackathon rank, college fest role, sports/leadership position]

Extracurricular and Leadership (Optional)

Include this only if it is genuinely relevant or you have limited project content to show. Keep it to one or two lines.

  • [Role, e.g. Coordinator, Technical Fest / Student Council Member] — [College Name] | [Year], [one line on what you organised or led]

ATS Friendly Resume Template: 1-2 Years of Experience

This layout adds a Work Experience section above Projects and Education, and tightens the summary to lead with what you have actually done on the job rather than what you are seeking.

Header

[Your Full Name]

[City, State] | [phone number] | [professional email] | linkedin.com/in/[yourname]

Summary

[Job title] with [X] years of experience in [domain/function], specialising in [core skill 1] and [core skill 2]. [One line naming a concrete result, e.g. "Reduced report turnaround time by 30% by automating a manual Excel process."] Looking to bring [specific strength] to a [target role] position.

Skills

  • [Technical skill 1], [Technical skill 2], [Technical skill 3], [Technical skill 4]
  • [Tool/software 1], [Tool/software 2], [Tool/software 3]
  • [Domain-specific skill, e.g. Vendor coordination, SQL reporting, UI testing]

Work Experience

[Job Title] — [Company Name], [City] | [Month, Year] – Present

  • [Action verb] + [what you did] + [measurable result], e.g. "Handled 40+ client escalations weekly, resolving 90% within the same working day."
  • [Action verb] + [what you did] + [scope/metric, e.g. team size, budget, volume, frequency]
  • [Action verb] + [specific tool used] + [outcome tied to a number wherever possible]

[Previous Job Title, if applicable] — [Company Name], [City] | [Month, Year] – [Month, Year]

  • [Same structure: action + task + measurable outcome]

Education

[Degree Name] — [College Name], [City] | [Year of graduation] | CGPA: [X.X/10] or Percentage: [XX%]

Projects and Certifications

  • [Project or certification name] — [one line on scope/outcome], [Year]
  • [Second entry, same structure]

Common Mistakes That Break Parsing

Even a well-worded resume fails if the container around the words is wrong. These are the most frequent issues Naukri's own checker and general ATS documentation both flag.

Two-Column and Table-Based Layouts

A visually appealing two-column resume — skills on the left, experience on the right — is read by many parsers left-to-right across the whole line, which merges unrelated text into nonsense strings. Stick to one column.

Headers, Footers, and Text Boxes

Contact information placed inside a document header or a design text box is frequently skipped entirely, because many parsers only read the main body flow of the document.

Graphics, Icons, and Photos

A phone icon next to your number, a skill-rating bar, or a photo add nothing a parser can read, and in some systems a large embedded image can even cause the whole file to fail extraction. Save the visual polish for LinkedIn, where a photo and formatting are actually expected.

Uncommon Section Labels and Abbreviations

A heading like "What I Bring to the Table" instead of "Skills", or an abbreviation your college uses locally but no recruiter outside it recognises, does not register as the field the parser is looking for. Stick to the plain, standard label even if it feels less creative — Experience, Education, Skills, Projects, Certifications.

How to Verify Your Resume Before You Apply

Once your resume matches one of the templates above, run it through an actual checker rather than guessing. Naukri offers a free ATS Resume Checker that scores your file out of 100 and flags parsing issues, missing keywords against a job description you paste in, and formatting problems — see our full breakdown of what Naukri's ATS checker actually does before you rely on it. Keep in mind that a template only gets you past the parsing step; the words inside it still need to match the language of the job description you are applying against. Review how to pick the right resume keywords for the specific role, and if you are starting from a blank page, our resume format guide for freshers covers section-by-section wording in more depth than the template above.

A Quick Manual Check Before Any Software Check

Before you even upload it anywhere, copy the entire text of your resume and paste it into a plain text editor with no formatting, such as Notepad. If the text comes out in the correct reading order — name first, then contact details, then each section in sequence, with no jumbled fragments from a sidebar or table — your layout is very likely to parse correctly elsewhere too. If sentences from your "Skills" column and your "Experience" column interleave into nonsense, that is the same failure an ATS parser will hit, and it is a strong sign the layout needs to move to a single column before you send it anywhere.

Building the Habit, Not Just the One Resume

Treat the template as a base file you maintain, not a one-time document you write once and forget. Every time you finish a new project, internship, or certification, add it to the base file immediately in the same format used above, with a measurable outcome wherever you can attach one. When you apply to a specific role, copy the base file, then adjust the Summary and Skills sections to mirror the language of that particular job description before you submit it. This keeps the structural formatting — the part that determines whether the parser can read it at all — untouched, while the content stays current and relevant to each application.

faq.q: What file format should an ATS friendly resume template use?
faq.a: Save it as a .docx file or a text-based PDF exported directly from Word or Google Docs. Never submit a scanned image or a PDF made from a photo of your resume — most parsers cannot extract text from it at all, so the application effectively arrives blank.

faq.q: Can a two-column resume template still be ATS friendly?
faq.a: No. Naukri's own resume-checker guidance flags two-column and table-based layouts as the single biggest cause of scrambled parsing, because many systems read text left-to-right across the full line width and merge unrelated columns into one string.

faq.q: Does an ATS friendly resume template need a specific font?
faq.a: Yes, stick to a standard, widely supported font such as Arial, Calibri, or Times New Roman at 10-12pt. Decorative or uncommon fonts can render incorrectly or fail to extract in some parsers.

faq.q: How long should an ATS friendly resume be for a fresher versus someone with 1-2 years of experience?
faq.a: A fresher resume should fit one page. With 1-2 years of experience, one full page or a little over is fine once you have a genuine Work Experience section, but avoid stretching content to fill two pages.

faq.q: Should I use the same ATS friendly resume template for every job I apply to?
faq.a: Use the same structural template, but change the wording. Swap in the specific skills and terminology from each job description, particularly in the Summary and Skills sections, since keyword match against that specific posting matters as much as the layout.

faq.q: Where can I check if my resume actually passes ATS parsing?
faq.a: Naukri's free ATS Resume Checker will score your resume, flag layout issues, and compare it against a job description you paste in. Running it before you apply is faster than guessing which template rule you may have broken.

title: Capgemini Interview Questions (2026): Exam Pattern & Answers
h1: Capgemini Interview Questions for 2026: Exam Pattern, Explained
seo_title: Capgemini Interview Questions 2026: Pattern & Salary
seo_description: Capgemini interview questions for 2026: pseudocode exam pattern, Analyst vs Senior Analyst salary tracks and sample answers. Start prepping this week.
excerpt: A section-by-section look at Capgemini's 2026 online test and track system — Analyst, Star Analyst, Senior Analyst — with salary data and real interview questions with sample answers.
content_html:
Capgemini's fresher hiring runs on a single online assessment that auto-sorts you into a pay track before you sit any interview, which is what most capgemini interview questions searches are actually trying to understand. The test has four timed sections — pseudocode (tracing data-structure and algorithm logic), quantitative aptitude, a game-based aptitude round that replaced older MCQ-style reasoning, and English communication — followed by either an essay or group discussion, then a technical interview and an HR round. Eligibility needs roughly 60% or 6.0 CGPA across Class 10, 12 and graduation with no active backlogs. Performance on the online test decides whether you land in the Analyst track (reported ₹4.0–4.25 LPA) or the higher Senior Analyst / Star Analyst track (reported ₹5.75–7.5 LPA) — you don't choose your track, the assessment does.

How Capgemini's Track System Actually Works

Unlike Wipro or Cognizant, where the track (Turbo, GenC Next) is usually decided by which drive you apply to, Capgemini funnels everyone through the same online test and then splits candidates into pay bands based on how well they scored — commonly referenced as Analyst, Star Analyst, and Senior Analyst tracks in recent cycles. This means two candidates from the same college, same branch, same drive, can walk away with meaningfully different offers purely based on test performance, not a separate application choice.

Eligibility criteria

CriterionRequirement
DegreeB.E./B.Tech, M.E./M.Tech, MCA, or M.Sc in CS/IT
Academic scoreMinimum 60% (or 6.0 CGPA) in Class 10, 12, and graduation
BacklogsNo active backlogs at the time of the recruitment drive
Experience noteRequirements can vary slightly by specific role or experience-level drive

Capgemini Exam Pattern: Section by Section

SectionQuestions/FormatDuration
Pseudocode~25 questions (data structures and algorithms logic-tracing)~25 min
English~30 questions~30 min
Game-based Aptitude4 mini-games replacing traditional MCQ reasoning~27 min total
Personality/Psychometric~100 statementsUntimed

There's no negative marking on the online test. After this, Capgemini runs either an essay (300–400 words on a tech or general topic) or a group discussion depending on the drive, followed by a technical interview covering programming, data structures and OS basics, and finally an HR interview.

The pseudocode section is the real differentiator

Because pseudocode tests your ability to trace logic rather than write syntax, it rewards candidates who can mentally execute loops and conditionals accurately under time pressure — this is also the section most closely tied to your eventual track placement, according to multiple 2025–26 prep-site breakdowns of Capgemini's process. Weak performance here is the single most common reason candidates land in the base Analyst band instead of Star or Senior Analyst.

Capgemini Salary: Analyst vs Star Analyst vs Senior Analyst

Capgemini doesn't publish exact cutoffs for which score lands you in which track, and reported CTC figures vary somewhat by source. The numbers below reflect a consolidated range across multiple 2025–26 candidate-reported breakdowns.

TrackReported CTCReported monthly in-hand
Analyst₹4.0–4.5 LPA₹28,000–34,000
Star Analyst~₹5.75 LPA₹42,000–50,000
Senior Analyst (selective)₹6.5–7.5 LPA₹55,000–65,000

Because track assignment is automatic and opaque, the only lever you fully control is your online-test score — there's no negotiation step at the offer stage the way there might be for a lateral hire. If you do get an offer and want to sanity-check what it means month to month, use the in-hand salary calculator and compare it against our CTC vs in-hand salary explainer before accepting.

Capgemini's 2026 Hiring Context

Capgemini India's leadership said in 2025 it planned to hire up to 45,000 people that year with an explicit focus on building an "AI-ready workforce," a figure widely reported by outlets including Storyboard18 and AI CERTs News. That hiring intent has continued to shape drives running into 2026: expect Capgemini's technical interviews to probe not just core CS fundamentals but also basic familiarity with AI-assisted development tools, since that's the stated direction of the company's workforce strategy. It doesn't change the exam pattern described above, but it's a reasonable signal for how to frame your "why Capgemini" answer and what to mention if you've used AI coding assistants in your own projects.

Common Mistakes That Get Freshers Rejected at Capgemini

  • Skipping pseudocode practice because it "sounds easy." Pseudocode questions look approachable on first read but are designed to be traced under time pressure — candidates who don't practise the trace-table method specifically tend to run out of time rather than get stuck on difficulty.
  • Ignoring the game-based aptitude section entirely. Because it's unfamiliar to most first-time test-takers and doesn't resemble typical campus-training material, walking in cold to this format costs candidates marks they'd otherwise easily get.
  • Assuming a good online-test score guarantees Senior Analyst placement. Track assignment criteria aren't published by Capgemini, and multiple sources give different score-to-track mappings — don't bank your financial planning on a specific track before you have an actual offer letter.

Real Capgemini Interview Questions With Sample Answers

Pseudocode-style

  • Q: Trace this algorithm and predict the final value of the variable after the loop terminates (a typical Capgemini pseudocode prompt with a counter and conditional break). Practice these by writing a small trace table — variable name, value at each iteration — rather than trying to run the logic mentally in one pass; that's exactly the discipline this section is testing.
  • Q: What is the time complexity of a binary search tree lookup in the worst case?
    A: "O(n) in the worst case, if the tree is completely unbalanced and effectively becomes a linked list. In a balanced tree, it's O(log n). I'd mention that self-balancing variants like AVL or Red-Black trees exist specifically to avoid that worst case."

Technical interview

  • Q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
    A: "A process has its own separate memory space and is heavier to create and switch between. A thread shares memory with other threads in the same process and is lighter-weight, so multithreading is generally more efficient for tasks that need to share data, but it introduces synchronization risks like race conditions that a process-based approach avoids."
  • Q: Explain your final-year project's biggest technical challenge.
    A: Name one specific bug or bottleneck (a slow query, a memory leak, a race condition) and how you diagnosed and fixed it — Capgemini's technical interviewers consistently rate specific debugging stories above high-level project summaries.
  • Q: What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?
    A: "SQL databases are relational, with a fixed schema and strong consistency guarantees — good for structured data like transactions. NoSQL databases (document, key-value, graph) trade some consistency guarantees for flexible schemas and horizontal scalability, which suits unstructured or fast-changing data like logs or user activity streams. I'd pick based on how rigid the data structure is and how much the app needs to scale reads versus writes."

HR round

  • Q: Are you okay with variable project allocation across domains — you might not get your first-choice technology?
    A: Answer with genuine flexibility but ask one clarifying question back (e.g., how allocation decisions are typically made) — this signals engagement rather than passive agreement. Our HR interview questions guide covers more variations of this fit-testing question style.
  • Q: What's your expected salary?
    A: Since track placement at Capgemini is decided by your test score rather than negotiation, the safer answer is to state that you're open to the standard package for your track and are more focused on the role and learning curve — naming a specific number you can't actually influence tends to come across as uninformed about how Capgemini's process works. Our expected CTC question guide covers how to handle this more generally.

How to Prepare: A Worked Example

Take a final-year Electronics and Communication student in Coimbatore with a 6.4 CGPA who's never written pseudocode-style questions before. Given that track placement is test-score-driven, the prep priority should be different from a company where interviews matter more:

  • Weeks 1–2: Daily pseudocode-tracing practice (20–25 problems a day) since this section most directly affects which pay track you land in, not just whether you clear the assessment. Pair with basic quantitative aptitude revision — profit and loss, time and work, and number series come up consistently.
  • Week 3: Practice the game-based aptitude format specifically — it's unfamiliar to most first-time test-takers and unlike anything in typical campus-training material, so a few timed practice attempts on the actual format matter more than generic reasoning practice here. Also start basic SQL and DBMS revision even if your branch isn't CS/IT, since the technical interview covers it regardless of the online test's exact section split.
  • Week 4: Prepare one strong essay/GD topic structure (a tech trend like AI in software delivery, argued with two concrete points and a conclusion) and rehearse your project's technical-challenge story for the interview stage. If you're deciding between Capgemini and another IT-services offer once results are in, our Infosys interview questions guide is a useful comparison point for a similar-scale process. If you're applying outside your own college's placement cell, budget extra time to track down drive announcements yourself — off-campus candidates typically get less advance notice than students at colleges with an active Capgemini tie-up.

Because Capgemini's track assignment happens automatically off your test score, treating the online assessment — especially pseudocode — as the actual interview, and the later rounds as confirmation, is the more accurate way to prepare. A candidate who scrapes through the assessment and interviews well can still land in the base Analyst track purely on test score, which is a harder outcome to plan around financially if you haven't budgeted for it going in. Whichever track you land in, don't skip verifying the exact number on your signed offer letter against what a recruiter told you verbally — variable pay components and joining bonuses are sometimes described loosely in phone calls and then itemised very differently in the actual annexure.

faq.q: How does Capgemini decide which salary track I get?
faq.a: Everyone takes the same online assessment, and your score on it — particularly the pseudocode section — determines whether you're placed into the Analyst, Star Analyst, or Senior Analyst track. There's no separate application step for higher tracks; it's decided by test performance, not a choice you make upfront.

faq.q: What is the Capgemini exam pattern in 2026?
faq.a: Four timed sections: pseudocode (about 25 questions, 25 minutes), English (about 30 questions, 30 minutes), a game-based aptitude round (4 mini-games, about 27 minutes total), and an untimed personality/psychometric section (around 100 statements). There's no negative marking, followed by an essay or group discussion, then technical and HR interviews.

faq.q: What CGPA is required for Capgemini interviews?
faq.a: The consistently reported minimum is 60% or 6.0 CGPA across Class 10, Class 12, and graduation, with no active backlogs at the time of the drive. Exact requirements can vary slightly by specific role or experience-level track, so confirm against your drive's notification.

faq.q: What is Capgemini's fresher salary in 2026?
faq.a: Reported ranges are ₹4.0–4.5 LPA for the Analyst track, around ₹5.75 LPA for Star Analyst, and ₹6.5–7.5 LPA for the more selective Senior Analyst track. These are candidate-reported planning ranges, not figures Capgemini has officially confirmed — your signed offer letter is the only authoritative number.

faq.q: Which section of the Capgemini test matters most?
faq.a: Pseudocode. It tests your ability to trace algorithm logic accurately under time pressure, and multiple 2025–26 prep-site breakdowns identify it as the section most closely tied to which pay track you land in, more than the English or personality sections.

faq.q: Is there negative marking in the Capgemini online test?
faq.a: No. Capgemini's online assessment has no negative marking across its pseudocode, English, and game-based aptitude sections, so attempting every question is generally the better strategy compared to skipping ones you're unsure about.

title: Entry Level Jobs India: 2026 Salary Bands and Sectors Hiring
h1: Entry Level Jobs India: What Freshers Can Realistically Expect
seo_title: Entry Level Jobs India 2026: Salary Bands by Sector
seo_description: Entry level jobs India 2026: real salary bands by sector, which cities are hiring, and how off-campus differs from placements. Start your search today.
excerpt: Entry-level pay in India ranges from ₹3.5 LPA to ₹18 LPA depending on sector and channel. Here is a realistic, sector-by-sector breakdown of where freshers are actually landing jobs in 2026, grounded in current hiring data.
content_html:
Searches for entry level jobs india usually turn up a confusing spread of numbers, and that spread is real: IT services roles at TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and Cognizant typically start between ₹3.5-7 LPA, while entry-level roles at product companies, GCCs (global capability centres), and high-growth sectors like AI/ML pay considerably more, often ₹8-18 LPA for the right skill set. According to Naukri's JobSpeak report for June 2026, fresher hiring grew 8% year-on-year and the April-June quarter grew 9% YoY, with AI/ML roles up 25% YoY, insurance up 16%, and telecom fresher hiring surging 25% YoY. The market for freshers is genuinely better than it was a couple of years ago, but salary and role quality still vary enormously by sector, city, and whether you come through a campus drive or an off-campus application. This guide breaks down realistic entry-level pay bands, the sectors actually hiring, and where freshers are landing roles beyond the traditional IT-services route.

What counts as an entry-level job in India

In the Indian market, "entry-level" usually means 0-2 years of experience, and includes campus hires, off-campus fresher hires, and early-career lateral movers. It covers a wide spread: mass fresher hiring by IT services majors, smaller cohorts at product and SaaS companies, government and PSU entry roles filled through exams, and a growing set of GCC (Global Capability Centre) roles set up by multinational companies in cities like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Pune.

Why the range is so wide

A B.Tech graduate joining TCS as a trainee and a B.Tech graduate joining a GCC data team can both be called "entry-level," but their starting CTC can differ by ₹5-10 lakh. The difference usually comes down to sector, skillset, and hiring channel rather than raw qualification, which is why generic advice like "just apply to entry-level jobs" is not very useful without narrowing down which segment you are targeting.

Entry-level salary bands by sector

These are realistic starting ranges reported across current hiring trend coverage and salary aggregators for the Indian market in 2026. Actual offers vary by college tier, city, and individual negotiation, but this gives a working benchmark.

Sector / role typeTypical entry-level CTC (LPA)Where hiring is concentrated
IT services (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant, Accenture)₹3.5-7Chennai, Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kolkata
GCC / MNC captive centres (non-tech roles: finance, analytics, ops)₹6-12Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Gurugram, Pune
Product / SaaS companies (SDE, associate roles)₹8-18Bengaluru, Gurugram, Hyderabad, Pune, remote
AI/ML and data roles (fresher-adjacent)₹10-20Bengaluru, Hyderabad, remote-first startups
BFSI and insurance (entry analyst roles)₹4-9Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru, Pune
BPO / ITES (voice and non-voice)₹2.5-4.5NCR, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, tier-2 cities

Which sectors are actually hiring freshers right now

According to Naukri's June 2026 JobSpeak data, the sectors showing the strongest year-on-year fresher and overall hiring growth were AI/ML (25%), insurance (16%), FMCG (7%), telecom (6% overall, 25% for freshers specifically), real estate (5%), and BPO/ITES and pharma/biotech (4% each). White-collar hiring overall grew 6% YoY nationally in June 2026, with the strongest metro growth in Kolkata (+12%), Hyderabad (+11%), Chennai (+10%), and Bengaluru (+7%), alongside faster growth in emerging cities like Bhubaneswar (+21%), Indore (+15%), and Coimbatore (+10%).

Telecom and insurance: an underrated entry point

Telecom and insurance rarely come up when freshers think about entry-level jobs, but both showed strong fresher-hiring growth in 2026. These sectors hire for roles in operations, customer analytics, underwriting support, and digital sales, and tend to be less saturated with applicants compared to the flood of resumes going toward IT services and product-company openings.

Tier-2 and tier-3 cities are not dead ends

Cities like Bhubaneswar, Indore, and Coimbatore showed faster YoY hiring growth than several metros in mid-2026 data. GCCs and IT services companies have been expanding delivery centres outside the traditional Bengaluru-Pune-Hyderabad belt, partly to manage costs and partly because tier-2 talent pools have grown. If you are from a tier-2 or tier-3 college, this is a genuine argument for looking at roles based in these cities rather than assuming a metro posting is required for a good entry-level job.

Campus placements vs off-campus: two different entry points

For students still in college, campus placements remain the fastest, lowest-friction route into an entry-level job, since companies come to the college and shortlist directly. But not everyone gets a campus offer, and many strong candidates from colleges without major recruiter tie-ups have to build an off-campus pipeline instead. Off-campus hiring works the same way as any lateral hiring process: you apply through job portals, LinkedIn, or direct company career pages, and you compete against a much larger, unfiltered pool.

What changes without a campus offer

Without the built-in shortlist that campus placements provide, your resume has to do more work. A resume that clears ATS screening and matches the specific job description becomes far more important, since recruiters are scanning through hundreds of applications rather than a pre-filtered batch from your own college.

What Indian recruiters actually screen for at entry level

For most entry-level roles outside of core IT services mass hiring, recruiters are looking for three things beyond your degree: a resume that clearly states relevant skills and projects, evidence of practical work (an internship, a project, a certification tied to the role), and a CTC expectation that is realistic for your profile and city. Overstating expected CTC relative to the role band is one of the most common reasons entry-level candidates get filtered out early, even when their skills are a reasonable match.

The skills that actually move the needle

For technical entry-level roles, basic proficiency in one language plus a portfolio project consistently outperforms a long list of unused certifications. For non-technical entry-level roles (analyst, ops, BFSI), Excel fluency, communication, and domain-specific case studies (even self-driven ones) matter more than generic soft-skill claims on a resume.

A realistic first-year expectation

Most entry-level hires in India, regardless of sector, spend the first 6-12 months in a structured training or ramp-up phase before taking on independent work. IT services companies in particular run multi-week induction training before deployment onto a project. This is normal and not a sign you are behind — it is built into how large-scale fresher hiring works in India, especially at companies bringing in cohorts in the tens of thousands.

Government and PSU entry-level routes

Outside the private-sector channels covered above, a meaningful share of entry-level hiring in India still runs through government exams and PSU recruitment: bank PO exams, SSC CGL, and PSU technical or management trainee intakes. These roles typically pay less in headline CTC than a product-company offer but come with job security, defined pay scales, and allowances that change the real take-home picture. The trade-off is timeline: exam-based hiring cycles can run 6-12 months from notification to joining, which is a very different planning horizon compared to a corporate off-campus application that can close in weeks.

Who this route suits

Government and PSU entry routes tend to suit candidates who can commit to a longer, structured preparation cycle and who value stability over the faster but more volatile private-sector track. It rarely makes sense as a fallback picked up in the last month of a private-sector search, since the preparation depth required is different enough that a rushed attempt usually does not convert.

How to actually improve your odds at entry level

Beyond picking the right sector, a few concrete habits change outcomes at the entry level more than most candidates expect.

  • Match your resume language to the specific job description rather than reusing one generic version for every application.
  • Apply within the first few days of a posting going live — response rates drop sharply as applicant counts climb into the thousands.
  • Keep your CTC expectation anchored to the sector and city band above, not to anecdotal numbers you have seen shared online.
  • Treat internships, even short or unpaid ones, as a legitimate substitute for missing full-time experience on your resume.
  • Track every application in a simple spreadsheet so you can tell, after a few weeks, whether your targeting or your resume needs to change.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good salary for an entry-level job in India in 2026?

For IT services fresher roles, ₹3.5-7 LPA is typical. For product companies, GCCs, and AI/ML-adjacent roles, ₹8-18 LPA is realistic depending on skillset and city. Anything materially above this band usually involves a specialised skill, a strong portfolio, or a Tier-1 college pedigree.

Which sectors are hiring the most freshers right now?

Based on Naukri JobSpeak data for June 2026, AI/ML, insurance, telecom, FMCG, and BPO/ITES showed the strongest year-on-year fresher and overall hiring growth, alongside the continuing volume hiring from IT services majors.

Do I need to be in a metro city to get a good entry-level job?

No. Emerging cities like Bhubaneswar, Indore, and Coimbatore showed faster hiring growth than several metros in mid-2026 data, driven by GCC and IT services expansion outside the traditional metro belt.

Is it better to wait for campus placements or start applying off-campus early?

Do both in parallel where possible. Campus placements are usually faster and lower-friction, but building an off-campus pipeline early means you are not left with zero options if you do not get a campus offer.

How long does it take to get an entry-level job after graduating?

This varies widely by sector, resume quality, and how targeted the search is. Candidates applying consistently and correctly often see initial traction within 4-8 weeks; a search that drags on for six months or more without any screening calls usually points to a resume or targeting problem rather than a market problem.

Are BPO and ITES jobs a bad entry point?

Not necessarily. They pay less than IT services or product roles (typically ₹2.5-4.5 LPA), but they can be a reasonable short-term entry point for building work experience and communication skills before moving to a higher-paying role, especially in a tight job market.
