title: Google Docs Resume Template: The 5 Built-In Options, Ranked by ATS Safety
h1: Google Docs Resume Template: Which of the 5 Built-In Layouts Is Actually ATS-Safe
seo_title: Google Docs Resume Template: 5 Options Ranked (2026)
seo_description: A google docs resume template guide ranking all 5 built-in layouts by ATS safety, with step-by-step editing tips. Open Google Docs and pick the right one.
excerpt: Google Docs has five built-in resume templates, completely free, with no download paywall. Here's which of the five are safe for applicant tracking systems, which one to avoid, and exactly how to use them.
content_html:
A google docs resume template is one of five ready-made layouts — Coral, Modern Writer, Spearmint, Serif, and Swiss — built directly into Google Docs' own Template Gallery, free for anyone with a Google account. Open Google Docs, click "Template gallery" in the top right, and scroll to the Resumes row; no sign-up, no trial, no download paywall like the ones that trip people up on dedicated CV builders. The catch is that not all five are equally safe for applicant tracking systems: Serif uses a two-column layout that can scramble how an ATS reads your work history, while Coral, Modern Writer, Spearmint, and Swiss are closer to single-column and parse more reliably. Which one you pick matters more than the fact that it's free.

The five built-in templates, and which are ATS-safe

Google doesn't market these as a resume product, so there's no upsell, no locked download button, and no watermark to remove — a genuine difference from tools like Zety or Novoresume, where the free plan often stops working right at the PDF export step. But "built into Google Docs" doesn't automatically mean "safe for a bot to read." Here's how the five native templates actually behave when you think about ATS parsing rather than just looks.

TemplateLayoutATS riskBest for
CoralSingle column, coral section headersLowFreshers who want a hint of colour without layout risk
Modern WriterSingle column, fuchsia header blockLowContent, marketing, or writing-adjacent roles
SpearmintSingle column, heavy white spaceLowRoles where recruiters skim fast — sales, BD, ops
SerifTwo-column, sidebar for skills/contactHighOnly for resumes a human will read directly, e.g. a referral email attachment
SwissSingle column, bold black divider linesLowEngineering and analyst roles that want a clean, no-nonsense look

The two-column problem with Serif isn't unique to Google Docs — it's the same reason ATS-friendly resume template guides keep repeating the single-column rule. Many parsers read left to right, line by line, across the full page width. If your sidebar has your phone number and email, and your main column starts with your job title, the parser can stitch those together in the wrong order, and a recruiter never sees the mismatch because they're looking at a rendered PDF, not the raw parsed text the ATS stored.

How to actually use one, step by step

Finding the templates

In Google Docs, click Template gallery in the top right corner of the start screen, or go through Google Drive: New > Google Docs > From a template. Scroll past the meeting notes and letters sections to "Resumes." If you don't see the gallery option at all, your Google Workspace administrator (common on some college-issued education accounts) may have hidden it — in that case, open a personal Gmail-linked Drive instead.

Editing without breaking the format

Replace the placeholder name, headline, and dummy job entries directly in place; don't delete and retype from scratch, since that's how spacing and font consistency quietly breaks. Keep section headers (Experience, Education, Skills) in plain text rather than converting them to Google Docs' built-in "Heading" styles with decorative formatting — plain bold text in a consistent font is safer for parsing than styled headings that some parsers ignore or misclassify.

Exporting the final PDF

File > Download > PDF Document (.pdf). This is where Google Docs has a real edge over most "free" builder tools: there's no download screen asking you to upgrade, no watermark, and no limit on how many times you export. You can also download as .docx if a specific application form asks for a Word file instead of a PDF, which some older Indian government or PSU recruitment portals still require.

Where Google Docs falls short of a dedicated resume tool

Being free and paywall-free doesn't mean Google Docs is the best tool for every situation. It has no built-in ATS score checker, no keyword matching against a job description, and no guardrails stopping you from adding a photo, a graphic skill-bar, or a two-column layout that undoes your own formatting discipline. If you want that kind of feedback loop, a checker built around Naukri-style Indian portals is a better fit than trusting a template's reputation, and it's worth running your exported PDF through one before you rely on Google Docs alone for a high-stakes application.

There's also no autosave-to-multiple-versions workflow the way some builders offer for tailoring a resume per job. In Google Docs, you do this manually: File > Make a copy, rename it per company, and keep a single "master" version you copy from every time so small edits in one tailored copy don't quietly drift into your main resume.

Google Docs vs. a free CV maker tool

Both routes are free, but they solve different problems. Google Docs has zero trial-and-cancel risk since there's never a payment screen to accidentally leave running, which matters given how often dedicated tools bury a recurring charge behind a "free" landing page. A dedicated builder, on the other hand, can offer AI-suggested bullet phrasing, live ATS scoring, and pre-built formatting rules that stop you from making a two-column mistake in the first place. If you're deciding between the two, our roundup of the best resume builders for the Indian job market breaks down which dedicated tools are worth the trade-off, alongside our separate look at which free CV maker tools genuinely let you download the PDF without hitting a paywall.

For most final-year students and freshers applying at scale — the volume campus placement season demands, where the same resume gets submitted to dozens of listings on Naukri or through off-campus drives — Google Docs' zero-risk, zero-cost model with a single-column template is the more defensible default. According to the India Skills Report 2026 covered by Careers360, national graduate employability reached 56.35% this year, up from 54.81% the year before, which means the gap between an average and a well-formatted resume is doing real work in a market where over 4 in 10 graduates still aren't considered employable by industry standards.

A worked example: turning Spearmint into a fresher resume

Start with the Spearmint template for a mechanical engineering fresher applying through campus placements. Replace the placeholder header with your name, phone number, email, and LinkedIn URL on one line, separated by pipes, not icons. Under "Education," list your degree, college, CGPA, and graduation year first, since for a fresher this carries more weight than a short internship. Under "Experience," reframe any internship using an action-plus-number structure ("Reduced changeover time on a test rig by 12% by rebuilding the fixture jig") rather than a duty list. Keep "Skills" as a plain comma-separated line, not the template's optional colour-coded proficiency bars, which some parsers read as decorative images rather than text. Export to PDF, then open the PDF itself and read it top to bottom as if you were a recruiter with 20 resumes stacked in a Naukri inbox and six seconds to decide.

Fixing the two most common Google Docs formatting problems

Font and spacing drift after copy-pasting

The single biggest way a Google Docs resume stops looking clean is copy-pasting text from a job description, an old resume in a different app, or a WhatsApp message directly into the template. Pasted text often carries its own hidden font and spacing formatting with it. Use "Paste without formatting" (Ctrl+Shift+V on Windows, Cmd+Shift+V on Mac) every time you paste text into any of the five templates, so it inherits the template's own font and size instead of fighting it.

Page breaks splitting a section awkwardly

If your resume runs slightly past one page, Google Docs will happily split a bullet point or a job title across the page break without warning you. Before exporting, scroll through the whole document and check that no entry is cut mid-sentence. If it's close to one page, trimming a weaker bullet point is almost always a better fix than shrinking the font size below 10.5pt, since undersized text creates its own readability problem for a human reviewer even if an ATS parses it fine.

Common mistakes people make with Google Docs resumes

  1. Keeping Serif's two-column layout for an online application. It looks organised on screen and can parse badly the moment it hits an ATS.
  2. Leaving the template's placeholder text half-edited. Recruiters do notice a stray "Lorem ipsum" or a template's example job title left in a bullet.
  3. Sharing the Google Doc link instead of the exported PDF. A live, editable Doc link can be seen as unfinished or unprofessional for a job application, and formatting can shift depending on the viewer's own Docs settings.
  4. Not checking file size and name. Export with your name in the file name (e.g., "Ananya_Sharma_Resume.pdf"), not the default "Resume - Copy.pdf" Google Docs suggests.
  5. Assuming free means finished. A Google Docs template still needs the same structure discipline as any other resume — a proven resume format for freshers matters more than which of the five templates you started from.
  6. Using the default template font at an unusual size. Some templates default to 11pt in a decorative font; switching to a standard font like Arial, Calibri, or Times New Roman at 10.5–11.5pt is a safer bet for both human readability and machine parsing.

When a Google Docs template isn't the right choice

There are a few situations where reaching for a dedicated tool instead of Google Docs makes sense. If you're applying to dozens of roles across different functions and need several meaningfully different versions tracked without manually renaming copies, a builder with saved-version management saves real time. If you specifically want an AI-generated first draft of your bullet points rather than writing every line yourself, that's also outside what Google Docs offers natively. And if a specific target company is known to use a particular ATS that's picky about formatting, testing your exported PDF against a dedicated ATS checker before relying on a plain Google Docs export is worth the extra step, since no template — free or paid — is automatically guaranteed to parse perfectly everywhere.

faq.q: Is the Google Docs resume template really free with no hidden download charge?
faq.a: Yes. All five templates in Google Docs' own Template Gallery (Coral, Modern Writer, Spearmint, Serif, Swiss) are free to use and export as a PDF via File > Download, with no watermark, no trial, and no card required, unlike several dedicated resume builders that let you design for free and then charge at the download step.

faq.q: Which Google Docs resume template is most ATS-friendly?
faq.a: Coral, Modern Writer, Spearmint, and Swiss are single-column layouts that tend to parse cleanly through applicant tracking systems. Serif uses a two-column sidebar layout, which carries a higher risk of an ATS misreading your contact details or work history order, so it's better suited to resumes that will be read directly by a person rather than scanned by software first.

faq.q: How do I find the resume templates inside Google Docs?
faq.a: Open Google Docs and click 'Template gallery' in the top right of the start screen, or go to Google Drive, click New, choose Google Docs, then 'From a template.' Scroll down to the Resumes section. If the gallery option is missing, it may be disabled on a college-managed Workspace account; use a personal Google account instead.

faq.q: Can I convert a Google Docs resume template to Word format?
faq.a: Yes. Use File > Download > Microsoft Word (.docx) instead of PDF. This is useful for older Indian government or PSU recruitment portals that specifically ask for a Word file rather than a PDF.

faq.q: Should I use a Google Docs template or a dedicated free CV maker tool?
faq.a: Google Docs has no paywall risk at all, which matters since several dedicated builders let you design a resume for free and then block the PDF download until you start a paid trial. A dedicated tool can offer AI phrasing help and live ATS scoring that Google Docs doesn't have, so the right choice depends on whether you want zero risk or extra guardrails; see our breakdown of free CV maker tools and their actual download policies for specifics.

title: Civil Engineer Resume Format for Indian Freshers (2026)
h1: Civil Engineer Resume Format: A Full Guide for Indian Freshers
seo_title: Civil Engineer Resume Format for Indian Freshers (2026)
seo_description: See the civil engineer resume format Indian recruiters check across site and design tracks, with a worked example and 2026 salary bands. Build yours today.
excerpt: The civil engineer resume format Indian recruiters actually screen for, split by site-execution and design tracks — a full worked example, real tools, and fresher salary bands sourced from 2026 data.
content_html:
A civil engineer resume format that works in India puts Education and site/design software (AutoCAD, STAAD Pro, Revit) above a career objective, and separates site-execution skills (billing, quantity surveying, supervision) from design-side skills (structural analysis, estimation), because Indian recruiters for this role split cleanly into two hiring tracks — construction/site roles at firms like L&T, Shapoorji Pallonji, and NCC, and government roles filled through GATE or state-level AE/JE exams — and each track screens for a different half of your skill set. Civil hiring has almost nothing in common with IT hiring: there's no coding round, campus placement packages are modest compared to CSE, and a large share of real entry-level demand sits in government exams rather than private-sector resume screening. Below is a full worked resume, the exact tools recruiters check in 2026, and salary bands drawn from sources actually checked, split by entry route.

How Civil Engineering Hiring Actually Works in India

Civil engineering freshers enter the workforce through three distinct routes, and each expects a slightly different resume emphasis.

Private construction and infrastructure firms (L&T, Tata Projects, Shapoorji Pallonji, Afcons Infrastructure, NCC, GMR) hire site engineers, billing engineers, and design-desk juniors both through campus placement drives and direct Naukri applications. These roles screen heavily for practical site skills — reading structural drawings, basic billing/quantity surveying, and supervising labour and subcontractors — over pure design software fluency.

Government roles — SSC Junior Engineer (JE), state PWD Assistant Engineer (AE), RRB JE, and various state PSC exams — are filled primarily through a written exam, not a resume screen, and represent a genuinely large share of civil engineering employment in India given the scale of public infrastructure. A resume matters here mainly at the interview/document-verification stage, not for shortlisting.

Design consultancies and PSU trainee programmes (via GATE for PSUs like NHAI-linked bodies, or direct hiring at structural consultancies) screen for AutoCAD, STAAD Pro, and IS-code familiarity more heavily, since the work is drawing- and calculation-based rather than site-based.

Know which of these three you're targeting before you write the resume — a site-engineer resume and a design-desk resume should not read identically.

The Right Section Order for a Civil Engineer Resume

1. Header

Name, phone, professional email, city, LinkedIn. No photo, no personal details beyond contact information.

2. Career Objective (optional, 2 lines)

State your target track explicitly — site execution or design — rather than a generic line. Example: "Civil engineering graduate with AutoCAD and STAAD Pro exposure from a 5-month structural design internship, seeking an entry-level design engineer role."

3. Education

B.Tech/B.E. Civil first, with college, CGPA/percentage, year — then Class XII and X. Government-exam applicants should also list eligibility-relevant details (percentage cutoffs vary by exam and matter at the document-verification stage).

4. Technical Skills

Split into Design/Software and Site/Execution categories so a recruiter can tell at a glance which track you're built for — see the table below for what's actually checked.

5. Internships and Projects

Site internships (even unpaid, through a family contact or college tie-up) carry real weight here, because "has actually stood on a site" is a genuine screening question at construction firms. Academic design projects matter more for the consultancy/design track.

6. Certifications

NPTEL courses on structural analysis or geotechnical engineering, and any AutoCAD/Revit/STAAD certification, should be listed with issuing body and year.

7. Achievements

Any technical fest participation, NSS/NCC (relevant for some government roles), or a paper presented — briefly, at the end.

A Full Worked Civil Engineer Fresher Resume

Ananya Sharma

Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh | +91-98XXXXXX47 | ananya.sharma@email.com | linkedin.com/in/ananyasharma

Career Objective

B.Tech Civil Engineering graduate with hands-on site execution experience from a 6-month internship on a residential building project, and working knowledge of AutoCAD and basic billing procedures, seeking an entry-level site engineer role.

Education

B.Tech, Civil Engineering — Institute of Engineering & Technology, Lucknow | 2026 | CGPA: 7.4/10

Class XII (UP Board) — 2022 | 81%

Class X (UP Board) — 2020 | 86%

Technical Skills

  • Design software: AutoCAD 2D/3D, basic STAAD Pro (coursework level)
  • Site/execution: Reading structural and architectural drawings, bar bending schedules, basic billing and measurement book (MB) entries, material reconciliation
  • Estimation: Quantity take-off for RCC and brickwork, basic rate analysis
  • Standards: Working familiarity with relevant IS codes for concrete and steel design
  • Other: MS Excel (BOQ tracking), MS Project (basic scheduling)

Internship — Site Engineer Intern, [Construction Contractor], Lucknow (Jan–Jun 2025)

  • Supervised daily shuttering and reinforcement work for a 4-floor residential slab pour, cross-checking bar bending schedules against structural drawings before each pour
  • Maintained measurement book entries and material reconciliation for cement and steel, flagging a 6% over-consumption issue against the BOQ that the site-in-charge traced to wastage at the mixing point
  • Assisted in preparing a running bill for a subcontractor package, verifying quantities against site measurements before submission to the billing engineer

Academic Project — Structural Design of a G+3 RCC Framed Building (Final Year, 2025–26)

  • Designed slab, beam, column, and footing sections per IS 456 for a G+3 residential structure using manual calculations cross-checked in STAAD Pro
  • Prepared full working drawings in AutoCAD, including a bar bending schedule for the ground-floor slab

Certifications

  • NPTEL — Design of Reinforced Concrete Structures (2025)
  • [Platform] — AutoCAD Civil Certification (2025)

Achievements

Runner-up, college technical fest structural-model competition (2024) — team lead for a scaled truss-bridge model tested under progressive load.

Skills and Tools Indian Recruiters Actually Screen For in 2026

Job-description keyword analysis of civil engineering postings (Jobscan's 2026 skills data) and what construction-firm site managers actually ask at interview converge on a short, practical list — and it splits cleanly by track.

Skill / ToolWhich track checks itWhy it matters
AutoCAD (2D/3D) / Civil 3DBoth tracksThe baseline drawing tool across nearly every Indian civil employer, from site to design desk
STAAD ProDesign/consultancy trackStandard structural analysis software at design consultancies and PSU design roles
Revit / BIM basicsLarger design consultancies, growing fastIncreasingly expected at bigger firms moving toward BIM-based project delivery
Bar bending schedules and reinforcement detailingSite track, near-universal interview questionDirectly tests whether you can read a drawing and translate it to actual site work
Billing / quantity surveying / MB entriesSite trackContractors hire site/billing engineers specifically to manage this day to day
IS code familiarity (IS 456, IS 875, etc.)Design track, and asked at most technical interviewsIndian structural design is governed by IS codes; not knowing the relevant ones is an immediate red flag
MS Excel and MS ProjectBoth tracksBOQ tracking and basic scheduling still run largely on Excel and Project across Indian sites

What Civil Engineering Fresher Salaries Actually Look Like in India

Civil fresher pay depends heavily on route, and the government-exam track pays meaningfully more than most private entry-level roles once cleared. Findmycollege.com's 2026 civil engineer starting-salary breakdown puts SSC Junior Engineer (JE) pay at roughly ₹4-5.5 LPA and state PSC Assistant Engineer (AE) roles at ₹6-8 LPA, while PSU roles at bodies like IOCL, ONGC, and NTPC (accessed via GATE or direct PSU recruitment) can reach ₹12-18 LPA. On the private side, the same source cites top-tier construction firms (L&T, Tata Projects, Afcons) touching around ₹6 LPA for strong campus hires, with most private entry-level site and design roles landing in the ₹3.5-6 LPA band. Separately, civilguide.in's 2026 salary data for civil freshers puts the broader 0-1 year range at roughly ₹2.2-4.2 LPA, with diploma holders typically starting lower (₹1.8-3.6 LPA) than B.Tech graduates in similar site-supervisor and junior-engineer roles.

Entry routeTypical fresher CTC (2026)Notes
Private site/junior engineer (general)₹2.2–4.5 LPAWidest volume of entry roles; diploma holders often start at the lower end
Top-tier construction firm (campus, e.g. L&T)Around ₹5–6 LPABest campus offers cluster near the top of this band
SSC Junior Engineer (JE)₹4–5.5 LPAExam-based; includes government job security and allowances
State PSC Assistant Engineer (AE)₹6–8 LPAExam-based, state-specific process and cutoffs
PSU (GATE or direct, e.g. IOCL, ONGC, NTPC)₹12–18 LPAHighest-paying route but the most competitive to clear

Run any of these CTC figures through our in-hand salary calculator before comparing offers, since government-role deductions and private-sector PF/tax structures differ.

Common Mistakes That Get Civil Engineer Resumes Rejected

Not Specifying a Track

A resume that reads as generically "civil engineer" without signalling site or design orientation makes a recruiter guess, and a site manager hiring for a construction role will pass on a resume that reads like a design-desk CV, and vice versa.

No Real Site Exposure Mentioned

For construction-firm roles, "has never actually been on a live site" is one of the fastest ways to get filtered out at interview, even with a strong CGPA. Any site visit, internship, or even a documented college site-survey exercise should be named explicitly.

Listing Software Without IS Code Awareness

STAAD Pro and AutoCAD proficiency without any mention of the governing IS codes for the work you did signals surface-level tool use rather than actual design understanding, and interviewers will probe this directly.

Overlooking the Government-Exam Track Entirely

Many civil freshers build a resume purely for private-sector applications and never mention exam preparation (SSC JE, state AE) even when actively studying for it — if that's your real plan, a short note under Achievements or a separate "Exams Cleared/Attempted" line can matter at interviews for hybrid profiles.

Tailoring This Format by Entry Route

If you're applying to construction firms and off-campus drives, lead with site/billing skills and any real site exposure, and keep the design-software section brief. If you're targeting design consultancies or PSU design roles, foreground STAAD Pro, IS-code familiarity, and any structural design project, and keep site-execution details lighter. If your real plan is the government-exam route, the resume matters less for shortlisting and more for the interview stage — focus your energy on exam preparation, and keep the resume itself simple and accurate. For the general structural rules that apply across any entry-level Indian resume, see our resume format guide for freshers, and if you're also applying through large-company portals that run automated screening, check how to pass ATS screening.

faq.q: What is the correct civil engineer resume format for a fresher in India?
faq.a: A single-page, single-column resume with Education (including CGPA) placed near the top, followed by a Technical Skills section split into Design/Software and Site/Execution categories, then Internships/Projects with concrete outcomes, then Certifications. Which skills you emphasise should match whether you're targeting a site-execution role or a design-desk role.

faq.q: Should a civil engineering fresher target private companies or government exams?
faq.a: Both are real tracks, and they need different preparation. Private firms (L&T, Tata Projects, Shapoorji Pallonji) hire through campus placement and direct applications with a resume screen. Government roles (SSC JE, state PSC AE) are filled primarily through a written exam, where the resume matters mainly at the interview and document-verification stage, not for shortlisting.

faq.q: What software should a civil engineer resume list?
faq.a: AutoCAD is the near-universal baseline across both site and design tracks. STAAD Pro and increasingly Revit/BIM basics matter more for design consultancy and PSU design roles. Site-track resumes should emphasise practical skills — reading bar bending schedules, billing, quantity surveying — over software depth.

faq.q: What is a realistic starting salary for a civil engineer fresher in India?
faq.a: According to findmycollege.com's 2026 breakdown, private entry-level site and design roles typically land in the ₹3.5-6 LPA range, SSC Junior Engineer roles pay roughly ₹4-5.5 LPA, state PSC Assistant Engineer roles pay ₹6-8 LPA, and PSU roles (IOCL, ONGC, NTPC) reach ₹12-18 LPA. Civilguide.in's separate 2026 data puts the broader 0-1 year private-sector range at roughly ₹2.2-4.2 LPA.

faq.q: Does a civil engineer fresher resume need site experience to be considered?
faq.a: For construction-firm site roles, yes, in practice — hiring managers routinely filter out candidates with no documented site exposure at all, even with a strong CGPA. Any internship, site visit, or college site-survey exercise should be named explicitly rather than left out.

faq.q: Is IS code knowledge important on a civil engineer resume?
faq.a: Yes, especially for design-track roles. Indian structural design is governed by IS codes (IS 456 for concrete, IS 875 for loads, and others), and interviewers commonly probe whether a candidate who lists STAAD Pro or AutoCAD actually understands the codes behind the design, not just the software interface.

title: New Tax Regime vs Old Regime: Which One Should You Pick?
h1: New Tax Regime vs Old Regime: A Line-by-Line Comparison for FY 2026-27
seo_title: New Tax Regime vs Old Regime: FY 2026-27 Comparison
seo_description: New tax regime vs old regime for FY 2026-27, with slabs, the ₹75,000 standard deduction, the Section 87A rebate and a worked example. Check before you choose.
excerpt: A worked comparison of the new tax regime vs old regime for FY 2026-27 — slabs, standard deduction, the Section 87A rebate, and when each one actually wins.
content_html:
For most salaried employees choosing between the new tax regime vs old regime for FY 2026-27, the new regime wins if you don't claim large deductions like HRA, 80C investments or a home loan — its slabs are wider and, thanks to the Section 87A rebate, income up to ₹12,00,000 a year is effectively tax-free after the standard deduction. The old regime can still win if your HRA exemption, 80C investments (PF, ELSS, life insurance), and a home loan or NPS contribution together push your deductions past roughly ₹4–5 lakh. There's no universal right answer — it depends entirely on your own numbers — so this article walks through both slab structures, the rebate math, and a full worked comparison on a ₹10,00,000 salary so you can run your own.

The Slabs, Side by Side

Both regimes tax income in slabs, but the new regime has more slabs at lower rates and a much higher tax-free threshold before rebate is even applied.

Income SlabNew Regime RateOld Regime Rate
Up to ₹2,50,000NilNil
₹2,50,000 – ₹4,00,000Nil5%
₹4,00,000 – ₹5,00,0005%5%
₹5,00,000 – ₹8,00,0005%20%
₹8,00,000 – ₹10,00,00010%20%
₹10,00,000 – ₹12,00,00010%30%
₹12,00,000 – ₹16,00,00015%30%
₹16,00,000 – ₹20,00,00020%30%
₹20,00,000 – ₹24,00,00025%30%
Above ₹24,00,00030%30%

On top of the tax computed from these slabs, both regimes add a 4% health and education cess, and the same surcharge structure applies above ₹50 lakh of income in either regime. The real differences are the standard deduction, the rebate, and which exemptions and deductions you're allowed to claim underneath the slabs — not the surcharge rules.

Standard Deduction: ₹75,000 vs ₹50,000

Every salaried taxpayer gets a flat standard deduction against salary income, no bills or proof required. Under the new regime it's ₹75,000; under the old regime it's ₹50,000. This alone shifts ₹25,000 of income out of the taxable base if you pick the new regime, before you even look at slabs.

The Section 87A Rebate: Why "Up to ₹12 Lakh Tax-Free" Gets Repeated

Section 87A gives a rebate — not an exemption, a rebate that cancels out tax already computed — to taxpayers below a specific income threshold. Under the new regime, the rebate is up to ₹60,000, which fully cancels the tax liability for taxable income up to ₹12,00,000. Under the old regime, the rebate is a much smaller ₹12,500, cancelling tax only up to a taxable income of ₹5,00,000. This is the single biggest reason the new regime is now the default for most salaried employees without large deductions: it isn't that the slab rates in isolation are dramatically lower, it's that the rebate erases tax entirely for a much wider income band.

One important catch: this rebate applies only up to the exact threshold. Cross it by even a small amount — say, taxable income of ₹12,00,500 under the new regime — and you're taxed on the full slab-wise amount from ₹0, not just the excess over ₹12,00,000, though marginal relief provisions typically cap the extra tax to the amount by which you exceeded the threshold. This is a frequent point of confusion, so don't assume a small bonus or increment won't matter if you're right at the edge of ₹12,00,000.

What You Lose Under the New Regime

The new regime's simplicity comes at a cost: most exemptions and deductions available under the old regime aren't allowed under the new one. That includes:

  • HRA exemption — even if you pay significant rent, you can't claim it against taxable income under the new regime.
  • Section 80C — investments in EPF, PPF, ELSS, life insurance premiums and principal repayment on a home loan, up to ₹1,50,000/year, aren't deductible under the new regime.
  • Section 80D — health insurance premiums aren't deductible under the new regime.
  • Home loan interest (Section 24) — interest on a home loan for a self-occupied property, up to ₹2,00,000/year under the old regime, isn't available under the new regime.
  • LTA — leave travel allowance exemption on actual travel bills isn't available either.

If your salary structure and life stage genuinely use several of these — you're paying meaningful rent, you have an EPF/PPF/insurance habit already, or you're servicing a home loan — the old regime can still come out ahead even with its narrower slabs and smaller rebate, because the deductions reduce your taxable income before any slab is applied.

A Worked Comparison: ₹10,00,000 Annual Salary

Take a salaried employee earning ₹10,00,000 a year, with ₹1,80,000 in eligible old-regime deductions: ₹1,20,000 HRA exemption and ₹60,000 in Section 80C investments (EPF plus one insurance policy). No home loan.

StepNew Regime (₹)Old Regime (₹)
Gross Salary10,00,00010,00,000
Less: Standard Deduction75,00050,000
Less: HRA Exemption01,20,000
Less: Section 80C060,000
Taxable Income9,25,0007,70,000
Tax before rebate (slab-wise)32,50066,500
Section 87A Rebate32,500 (taxable income ₹9,25,000 is under the ₹12,00,000 threshold, so the full computed tax is rebated)0 (taxable income is above the old regime's ₹5,00,000 rebate threshold)
Tax after rebate066,500
Add: 4% Cess02,660
Final Tax Payable₹0≈₹69,160

In this specific case, the new regime wins decisively — because taxable income after just the standard deduction (₹9,25,000) stays under the ₹12,00,000 rebate threshold, the entire tax liability is wiped out by Section 87A. The old-regime taxpayer, even after claiming both HRA and 80C, still owes roughly ₹69,160. For the old regime to close this gap, this employee would need deductions large enough to bring taxable income down further, which typically requires a home loan or substantially higher rent and 80C investments than in this example. This is one worked scenario, not a universal outcome — run your own salary and actual deductions through the in-hand salary calculator before deciding, since the answer flips depending on your specific numbers.

When the Old Regime Still Wins

The old regime tends to come out ahead when several large deductions stack together — typically home loan interest (up to ₹2,00,000), a near-maximum HRA claim in a metro, and a full ₹1,50,000 of Section 80C investments. Add those up and you're often looking at ₹4,00,000–₹5,00,000 of deductions, which can bring taxable income low enough that the old regime's smaller rebate and higher rates still land below the new regime's tax. If you're a fresher without a home loan and minimal 80C investments so far, the new regime is very likely the better default — but if you already have a home loan or a well-established PF and insurance habit, it's worth running both calculations rather than assuming.

A Second Worked Example: ₹15,00,000 Salary With a Home Loan and High Rent

The gap narrows — and can even flip — once deductions get genuinely large. Take an employee earning ₹15,00,000 a year with a ₹6,00,000 annual basic, paying ₹25,000/month rent in a metro (a common situation for someone who owns a home financed by a loan in their hometown but works and rents in a different city), claiming the full ₹1,50,000 under Section 80C, and ₹2,00,000 of home loan interest under Section 24.

StepNew Regime (₹)Old Regime (₹)
Gross Salary15,00,00015,00,000
Less: Standard Deduction75,00050,000
Less: HRA Exemption02,40,000
Less: Section 80C01,50,000
Less: Home Loan Interest (Sec 24)02,00,000
Taxable Income14,25,0008,60,000
Tax before rebate (slab-wise)93,75084,500
Section 87A Rebate0 (taxable income above the ₹12,00,000 threshold)0 (taxable income above the old regime's ₹5,00,000 threshold)
Add: 4% Cess3,7503,380
Final Tax Payable≈₹97,500≈₹87,880

Here the old regime wins, but only by around ₹9,600 for the year — roughly ₹800 a month — despite stacking HRA, full 80C and the maximum home loan interest deduction. That margin is the honest picture: even with genuinely large, realistic deductions, the new regime's wider slabs and bigger rebate threshold have closed most of the old regime's traditional advantage. If your deductions are smaller than this — say, just 80C without a home loan — the new regime typically wins even at this income level. This is exactly why "just pick whichever regime saves more on paper for your specific numbers" beats any rule of thumb, including this article's own examples.

The One Deduction Both Regimes Allow: Employer NPS Contributions

Section 80CCD(2) — the deduction for an employer's contribution to your NPS account — is one of the few benefits available under both regimes, which is why it's frequently flagged as the new regime's one remaining lever. Under the old regime, private-sector employees can claim this deduction up to 10% of basic+DA; under the new regime, that limit rises to 14% of basic+DA for both private and government employees, a change introduced in a recent Budget. It only helps if your employer actually offers a structured NPS contribution as part of your CTC — it isn't something you can unilaterally claim by investing in NPS yourself under the new regime, that's a different provision (Section 80CCD(1B)) available only under the old regime. If you're negotiating a new offer and your CTC structure allows it, asking payroll to route a portion of your compensation through employer NPS is worth doing regardless of which regime you pick, precisely because it's one of the only levers that survives both.

Can You Switch Between Regimes Every Year?

Salaried employees without business income can switch between the new and old regime every financial year when filing their return, regardless of what they declared to their employer for TDS purposes during the year. If your employer over- or under-deducted TDS based on your declared regime, you reconcile the difference — refund or additional payment — at the time of filing. Self-employed individuals and those with business income have more restrictive switching rules, so this flexibility mainly benefits salaried employees.

How This Interacts With Your Salary Structure

Your regime choice also affects how your CTC should ideally be structured. Under the old regime, a higher HRA and a Section 80C-eligible structure (like an employer-facilitated NPS contribution) reduce your taxable income meaningfully. Under the new regime, those structuring choices barely matter for tax purposes since most exemptions aren't available — so a simpler, higher-Basic structure with fewer named allowances doesn't cost you anything under the new regime. If you're negotiating a new offer, understanding this can inform how you ask HR to structure your salary slip components, and how the PF portion in particular gets treated — see our PF deduction explainer for that piece specifically.

Tax rules change with every Union Budget — slabs, rebate thresholds and deduction limits have all moved in recent years, and they can move again. Verify the current figures against the Income Tax Department's official e-filing portal or a qualified tax professional before making a decision, and treat this article as general information rather than personalised financial advice.

faq.q: Which is better, the new tax regime or the old regime?
faq.a: It depends on your deductions. If you don't have significant HRA, 80C investments, or home loan interest to claim, the new regime almost always wins because of its higher standard deduction (₹75,000) and the Section 87A rebate, which makes taxable income up to ₹12,00,000 effectively tax-free. If your eligible deductions add up to roughly ₹4-5 lakh or more, the old regime can still come out ahead.

faq.q: Is income up to ₹12 lakh really tax-free under the new regime?
faq.a: For salaried taxpayers, taxable income (after the ₹75,000 standard deduction) up to ₹12,00,000 attracts a Section 87A rebate of up to ₹60,000, which cancels the computed tax entirely. Crossing the threshold removes the rebate, though marginal relief limits the extra tax to the amount by which you exceeded it. This is not the same as gross salary being tax-free — it applies to taxable income after the standard deduction.

faq.q: Can I switch between the new and old tax regime every year?
faq.a: Yes, if you're a salaried employee without business income — you can choose either regime each year when filing your return, independent of what you declared to your employer for TDS. Employees with business income face more restrictive switching rules.

faq.q: What deductions can I no longer claim under the new tax regime?
faq.a: The new regime removes HRA exemption, Section 80C (EPF, PPF, ELSS, insurance premiums), Section 80D (health insurance), home loan interest under Section 24, and LTA exemption, among others. You keep the flat ₹75,000 standard deduction and the employer's NPS contribution deduction, but most other exemptions are gone.

faq.q: Do tax slabs and the 87A rebate change every year?
faq.a: Yes — both have changed in recent Union Budgets and can change again. Always verify the current financial year's slabs, standard deduction and rebate threshold against the Income Tax Department's official guidance before filing or making a regime decision, rather than relying on a previous year's figures.

title: How ATS Software Works: Parsing, Filtering, Ranking Explained
h1: How ATS Software Works, Step by Step
seo_title: How ATS Software Works: A Step-by-Step Explanation
seo_description: See exactly how ATS software works — parsing, keyword search, and knockout rules — so you know what's really costing you interview calls. Read the breakdown.
excerpt: A step-by-step, myth-free explanation of how ATS software actually works — parsing, indexing, filtering, and ranking — and why most 'ATS rejection' claims are misunderstood.
content_html:
Here's how ATS software works: it reads your resume file, pulls the text out using optical character recognition and natural language processing, tags pieces of that text as "entities" — a company name, a date range, a degree, a skill — and drops each tagged entity into a searchable database field. It does not, by default, "score" or reject you on its own; a human recruiter searches and filters that database using keywords, date ranges, and yes/no knockout questions they set up themselves. According to Jobscan's manual review of Fortune 500 career pages, 97.8% of large employers run a detectable ATS of this kind, and the same parsing logic sits behind Naukri, LinkedIn, and most enterprise hiring systems used by large Indian recruiters. What breaks candidates is not a mysterious rejection algorithm — it is bad parsing, a keyword mismatch, or getting buried under volume.

What an ATS Actually Is

An applicant tracking system is recruiting software that stores every application a company receives, in one searchable place, instead of a folder of email attachments. Recruiters at Indian firms hiring at scale — think TCS or Infosys running a campus drive that pulls in tens of thousands of applications in a single cycle — could not physically open every file. The ATS lets them query the pool instead: "show me every candidate with 'SQL' and 'Power BI' in their resume, based in Bangalore, willing to relocate." Globally, the most common platforms by market share, based on Jobscan's analysis of more than a million resume scans across 12,820 companies, are Greenhouse (19.3%), Lever (16.6%), Workday (15.9%), and iCIMS (15.3%). In India, large enterprises more often run Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, or homegrown platforms like Darwinbox, while portals like Naukri run their own parsing layer for the resumes candidates upload directly.

Step One: Parsing — Turning a Document Into Data

The moment you upload a resume, the ATS does not "read" it the way a person does. It runs the file through a parser that extracts raw text, then applies Natural Language Processing techniques — specifically a method called Named Entity Recognition — to identify which chunks of text are which kind of thing: a person's name, a job title, a company, a date, a degree, a skill. This is the step where formatting choices matter enormously.

Why Layout Breaks This Step

A single-column resume with standard headings gives the parser a clean, linear stream of text to tag. A two-column layout, a table, or text inside a header or footer often gets read out of order or skipped entirely, because many parsers process the main body text flow and nothing else. The result is a candidate record with blank fields — no dates, no company names — even though the actual resume file looks perfectly fine to a human. For the exact formatting choices that avoid this, see our ATS friendly resume template.

Step Two: Indexing — Making the Data Searchable

Once your resume is parsed into fields, the system does not re-scan the original file every time a recruiter searches. It builds what is effectively a word-to-candidate map — an inverted index — so that when a recruiter searches "Python", the system instantly returns every candidate whose parsed record contains that word, rather than re-reading thousands of PDFs on demand. This is also how Boolean search works inside these systems: a recruiter can search "Python AND SQL NOT internship" to combine, include, or exclude criteria in one query.

Step Three: Filtering and Knockout Questions

This is the step most job seekers misunderstand. The ATS itself does not decide you are unqualified. A human recruiter or hiring manager configures rules in advance — commonly called knockout questions — such as "Do you have a minimum of 1 year of experience in customer support?" or "Are you willing to work rotational shifts?" If you answer in a way that fails the rule, the system moves your application to a rejected folder automatically, but the rule itself was set by a person, not invented by the software. A widely repeated claim online is that "75% of resumes are rejected by ATS" before a human ever sees them. This figure traces back to a 2012 marketing claim by a company called Preptel that published no methodology, sample size, or survey behind it — it is not a confirmed statistic, and we are treating it as an unverified industry claim rather than fact. A 2025 Enhancv survey of 25 recruiters across industries found that around 92% do not configure their systems to auto-reject resumes based on content or formatting at all; most auto-rejection is reserved for hard mismatches like work authorization or a missing mandatory certification.

OCR, and Why Scanned Resumes Fail Immediately

If your resume is a scanned image or a photograph saved as a PDF, the parser has to fall back on Optical Character Recognition to even attempt reading it, and OCR is far less reliable than reading text that was typed directly into the file. A resume exported straight from Word or Google Docs as a text-based PDF avoids this problem entirely, because the underlying text is already selectable and machine-readable — you can test this yourself by trying to highlight text in your own PDF before you submit it. If you cannot select individual words with your cursor, the file is almost certainly image-based and will parse badly.

Step Four: Ranking, and Why It Is Not Automatic Scoring

Some modern ATS platforms do offer a ranking or "match score" feature that estimates how closely a resume's parsed content aligns with a job description, and some also let interview panel members submit standardised scorecards that the system aggregates into a composite rating later in the process. But the baseline behaviour of an ATS is filtering and sorting, not independently judging candidate quality. If your resume seems to "score low," in most cases what actually happened is one of three things: your formatting caused a parsing failure (fields came out blank or garbled), your wording did not contain the terms the recruiter searched for, or your application is sitting correctly in the system but far down a list of hundreds of others for that posting. Understanding what counts as a good ATS score is more about matching a specific job description than hitting some universal number.

Where Human Judgement Re-Enters the Process

Once a resume clears parsing and shows up in a recruiter's filtered search, a person is reading it, not software. In larger Indian hiring processes — a TCS or Infosys campus drive, for instance — recruiters often work through shortlists in the ATS interface itself, adding notes, tagging candidates for specific interview panels, and, in more mature systems, collecting structured scorecards from each interviewer that the platform totals into a combined rating. That combined rating is a human-judgement aggregation tool, not the same as the earlier parsing or keyword-filtering steps. Confusing the two is where a lot of "the ATS rejected me" thinking goes wrong: by the scorecard stage, your resume already made it well past the software.

What people assumeWhat actually happens
"The ATS reads my resume like a human would"It extracts text and tags entities; layout errors cause blank or scrambled fields
"The ATS auto-rejects most resumes"Auto-rejection rules are set by a human recruiter for specific hard criteria, not by the software's own judgment
"There's one universal ATS score everyone is judged against"Matching is calculated against the specific job description a recruiter is filling, so the same resume scores differently for different roles
"A fancy visual resume proves I'm detail-oriented"Visual layouts (columns, graphics, icons) are the leading cause of parsing failures across ATS platforms
"Once I'm in the system, nothing else matters"Recruiters still actively search and filter using keywords, so wording continues to matter after you apply

How This Plays Out on Naukri Specifically

Naukri works slightly differently from a company's own ATS, because you are not applying to one job posting inside a closed system — you are maintaining a searchable profile that many recruiters query directly. Naukri does publish a free ATS-style resume checker that scores formatting and keyword match against a job description, but the separate "resume score" or "profile completeness" percentage you see on your dashboard measures how many profile fields you have filled in, not how well your resume would parse inside a company's actual ATS. We cover this distinction in detail in how Naukri's resume tools actually work, because conflating the two is one of the more common and costly misunderstandings among Indian job seekers.

Where This Matters Most in the Indian Hiring Cycle

Volume is the real bottleneck in Indian hiring, and it is why the ATS exists in the first place. A single off-campus drive or a popular listing on Naukri for a generic role — customer support, business development, entry-level software roles — can draw several hundred to a few thousand applications within days. No recruiting team reviews that volume manually. The ATS lets a two- or three-person recruiting team at a mid-size company do what would otherwise need a much larger team: narrow a few thousand applications down to a shortlist of thirty or forty worth reading closely, using search terms tied directly to the job description. That mechanical reality is also why generic, one-size-fits-all resumes underperform — they are less likely to contain the specific terms that surface in a narrow, well-targeted search.

What to Actually Do With This Information

Once you know an ATS is a search-and-filter tool rather than a judge, the practical response changes. Formatting has to be clean enough to parse without errors — that is a one-time fix, not an ongoing battle. After that, the real, repeatable work is making sure your resume's wording contains the specific terms a recruiter for that specific role is likely to search for, which changes job posting to job posting. That is a wording and research task, not a trick to "beat" software. Three things to do this week: run your current resume through a text-editor copy-paste test to confirm it parses cleanly, rewrite your Skills section to mirror the exact phrasing used in two or three real job postings you are targeting, and stop reusing one generic resume for every application if the roles differ even slightly in required skills.

faq.q: How does ATS software work in simple terms?
faq.a: It extracts the text from your resume file, tags pieces of it as entities like company names, dates, and skills using natural language processing, and stores that structured data so a recruiter can search and filter it later. It does not judge your resume on its own by default.

faq.q: Does an ATS automatically reject resumes?
faq.a: Not by default. A human recruiter configures specific knockout rules, such as a minimum experience requirement, and only applications that fail those explicit rules move to a rejected folder automatically. The widely repeated '75% of resumes get auto-rejected' claim traces back to an unsourced 2012 marketing statistic, not confirmed research.

faq.q: Which ATS platforms are most common among large employers?
faq.a: According to Jobscan's analysis of over a million resume scans across 12,820 companies, Greenhouse (19.3%), Lever (16.6%), Workday (15.9%), and iCIMS (15.3%) lead by market share. Large Indian enterprises commonly run Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, or Darwinbox, while Naukri uses its own parsing layer.

faq.q: Why does resume formatting matter so much if the ATS is just software?
faq.a: Because the very first step is parsing your file into text, and layout choices like tables, columns, headers, and graphics are the leading cause of that step failing. If parsing fails, every later step — search, filter, ranking — works with incomplete or wrong data.

faq.q: Is there one universal ATS score every job seeker should aim for?
faq.a: No. Matching is typically calculated against a specific job description, so the same resume can score well for one posting and poorly for another in an adjacent function. Tailoring wording to each job description matters more than chasing a single fixed number.

faq.q: Is Naukri's resume score the same as an ATS score?
faq.a: No, and this is a common confusion. Naukri's dashboard score largely reflects profile completeness and recency, which affects your visibility in recruiter searches on Naukri specifically, not whether your resume parses correctly inside a company's own ATS.

title: Cognizant Interview Questions (2026): GenC, GenC Next & Answers
h1: Cognizant Interview Questions for 2026: GenC vs GenC Next, Explained
seo_title: Cognizant Interview Questions 2026: GenC & GenC Next
seo_description: Cognizant interview questions for 2026: GenC vs GenC Next eligibility, salary, rounds and sample answers. Pick the right track for your drive today.
excerpt: A track-by-track guide to Cognizant's 2026 fresher hiring — GenC, GenC Next and GenC Elevate — with eligibility, salary data, and real interview questions with sample answers.
content_html:
Most cognizant interview questions searches are really about telling apart Cognizant's fresher tracks — GenC, GenC Next, and GenC Elevate (a specialist/PEGA-Salesforce-SAP track that some sources also call GenC Pro, though naming is inconsistent across hiring cycles and should be verified against your specific drive notification). GenC is the base track, open with programming knowledge "recommended but not mandatory," and runs a 60–90 minute aptitude test followed by a technical and HR interview. GenC Next is for stronger coders and adds a two-part written round — conceptual code analysis plus a coding section testing DSA, OOP and databases — followed by a mandatory three-month internship before a differential package kicks in. Eligibility across tracks needs roughly 60% in Class 10, 12 and graduation, no more than a one-year gap after Class 12, and no pending backlogs. Reported CTC is around ₹4 LPA for GenC and ₹6.5 LPA (some sources cite up to ₹6.75 LPA) for GenC Next — treat exact figures as reported-but-unconfirmed until your own offer letter.

GenC vs GenC Next vs GenC Elevate: What Actually Separates Them

Cognizant's track names have shifted across hiring cycles (GenC Pro, GenC Elevate and GenC Next have all been used slightly differently in different years' campus material), so don't anchor your prep on any one name without checking your current drive's brochure. The underlying logic, though, has stayed consistent.

GenC

The volume track. Cognizant explicitly states programming knowledge is recommended but not required, which tells you the written test leans harder on aptitude — analytical ability, abstract reasoning, numerical and verbal skills — than on hands-on coding. This is the entry point for most non-CS branches and candidates without strong prior coding exposure.

GenC Next

The stronger-coder track. It adds a two-section written assessment (roughly 30 minutes of conceptual code analysis, then about 70 minutes of coding covering data structures, OOP and databases), a longer technical interview, and — distinctively — a mandatory three-month internship before the higher, differential CTC is confirmed. If you're strong at DSA but weak on spoken English, GenC Next is still worth attempting; the written round weighs technical skill more heavily than GenC's.

GenC Elevate / specialist tracks (reportedly GenC Pro in some cycles)

Aimed at candidates with demonstrable exposure to specific enterprise platforms — PEGA, Salesforce, SAP, or cybersecurity — this track carries a reported salary premium over base GenC. Sources disagree on whether this track is currently branded "GenC Pro" or "GenC Elevate" for the 2026 cycle, and on exact CTC; some prep sites report GenC Elevate CTC close to base GenC (₹4.0–4.3 LPA) rather than a large premium, which contradicts the "specialist premium" framing elsewhere. Given this inconsistency, verify the current track name and its pay band directly on Cognizant's careers page for your specific drive rather than trusting any single prep-site figure.

Eligibility Criteria for Cognizant Interviews in 2026

CriterionRequirement
DegreeBE, B.Tech, ME, M.Tech, or MCA (full-time)
Academic scoreMinimum 60% in Class 10, Class 12, and graduation
Education gapNo more than one year after Class 12
BacklogsNo pending/active backlogs at the time of selection
GenC Next add-onStronger coding proficiency expected at written-test stage; no separate CGPA cutoff confirmed

Cognizant Interview Process: Round by Round

Stage 1: Written Test

GenC candidates typically sit a 60–90 minute aptitude test (analytical ability, abstract reasoning, critical thinking, numerical and verbal skills). GenC Next candidates sit a two-part test instead: about 30 minutes of conceptual/code-analysis questions, then about 70 minutes of coding testing DSA, OOP and database fundamentals — noticeably more technical than the GenC paper.

Stage 2: Technical Interview

20–30 minutes for GenC, closer to 30 minutes for GenC Next, covering your primary programming language, basic DSA, and a walkthrough of any project or internship on your resume. GenC Next interviews go deeper into problem-solving approach and code quality than GenC's.

Stage 3: HR Interview

Standard fit assessment — background, willingness to relocate/travel, and general industry awareness. Shorter than the technical round for both tracks.

Cognizant Salary: GenC vs GenC Next in 2026

Cognizant doesn't publish a single confirmed fresher CTC, and prep sites vary in their reported numbers by a meaningful margin. The ranges below reflect the spread across multiple 2025–26 sources.

TrackReported CTCReported monthly in-handNotes
GenC₹4.0 LPA₹28,000–32,000Widely and consistently reported
GenC Elevate₹4.0–4.3 LPANot separately confirmedSome sources report near-parity with base GenC, not a large premium
GenC Next₹5.4–6.75 LPA (varies by source)₹46,000–50,000Confirmed only after mandatory 3-month internship

Post-appraisal, GenC hikes to a reported ₹4.5–5 LPA and GenC Next to roughly ₹7.5–8.5 LPA after a strong first year, per multiple 2026 prep-site breakdowns — again unconfirmed by Cognizant directly. Before comparing offers across companies, run the actual number through a CTC vs in-hand salary calculation, since GenC's ₹4 LPA CTC and a similar-looking offer elsewhere can differ by a few thousand rupees a month depending on how Basic and allowances are structured.

Cognizant's 2026 Hiring Context: What "Project Leap" Means for Freshers

Worth knowing before you spend weeks prepping: Cognizant has been reported to be planning significant layoffs — figures cited in 2026 coverage range from around 12,000 to as many as 15,000 roles globally under an internal restructuring effort referred to as "Project Leap," with India expected to absorb a large share of the impact, according to reporting by American Bazaar Online and others in May 2026. Separately, other 2026 reports describe Cognizant cutting a smaller number of roles (around 4,000) while still hiring roughly 20,000 freshers in the same period — the two figures come from different reports and aren't fully reconciled in public coverage, so treat both as directional rather than confirmed. CEO Ravi Kumar S has publicly framed the shift as moving toward a "broader and shorter pyramid" that combines AI tooling with human delivery teams. The practical read: Cognizant is still actively recruiting freshers into GenC-track roles even while trimming elsewhere, but the bar for what a "junior" hire is expected to do — more AI-tool fluency, less pure manual coding — is shifting underneath the same track names.

Common Mistakes That Get Freshers Rejected at Cognizant

  • Applying to GenC Next without DSA fundamentals. The written test for this track is materially more technical than GenC's, and candidates who apply to it purely for the higher CTC without DSA practice tend to fail the code-analysis section specifically.
  • Assuming "programming not mandatory" means no technical interview. Even GenC's technical round still probes basic programming concepts and a project walkthrough — the "not mandatory" language applies to the written test's design, not to the entire process.
  • Not clarifying track names before a specific drive. Because Cognizant's specialist/premium track naming has shifted across recent cycles (GenC Pro in some material, GenC Elevate in others), candidates sometimes prep for the wrong pay expectations. Always check the specific brochure for your drive rather than a generic prep-site page.

Real Cognizant Interview Questions With Sample Answers

GenC written/aptitude style

  • Q: A shopkeeper marks up an item by 25% and then gives a 10% discount. What's the net profit percentage?
    A: Work it as multipliers: 1.25 × 0.90 = 1.125, so net profit is 12.5%. Cognizant's aptitude section rewards speed on exactly this kind of two-step percentage problem, so practice chaining multipliers instead of recalculating from scratch each step.

GenC Next coding/technical

  • Q: What's the difference between a stack and a queue, and where would you use each?
    A: "A stack is LIFO — last in, first out — useful for things like undo functionality or expression evaluation. A queue is FIFO — first in, first out — useful for task scheduling or a print queue. I used a stack in my project to implement bracket-matching validation for a mini code editor."
  • Q: Explain the difference between == and .equals() in Java (or the equivalent in your language).
    A: "== checks reference equality for objects — whether two variables point to the same memory location — while .equals() checks logical/value equality, which is what you usually want when comparing content like strings. I ran into this bug once comparing two String objects with == and got unexpected false results."

HR round

  • Q: Why do you want to join Cognizant?
    A: Reference something concrete — Cognizant's scale in BFSI and healthcare IT services in India, or a specific GenC track you're targeting and why it fits your skills — rather than a generic "good brand" answer. Pair this with our expected CTC question guide, since Cognizant recruiters often ask this directly in the same round.
  • Q: How do you handle working in a team where a member isn't pulling their weight?
    A: Give a real example — a college group project, a hackathon team — and describe the specific action you took (redistributing tasks, having a direct conversation) rather than a vague "I motivate them" answer. Cognizant's HR interviewers use this question to gauge conflict-handling maturity, which matters more in a services company where you'll be staffed on client teams from day one.

How to Prepare: A Worked Example

Take a final-year Information Technology student from a tier-2 college in Nagpur with a 6.8 CGPA, decent aptitude but shaky DSA. Since GenC weighs aptitude more than coding, this profile should target GenC first rather than stretching for GenC Next:

  • Weeks 1–2: Daily aptitude practice — percentages, ratios, time-speed-distance, logical/abstract reasoning puzzles — since GenC's written round is aptitude-heavy by design.
  • Week 3: Light DSA revision (arrays, strings, basic stack/queue/linked list) even for the GenC track, because the technical interview still probes fundamentals regardless of which written test you sat.
  • Week 4: Mock HR round focused on "why Cognizant" and salary-expectation questions, plus one full project walkthrough rehearsal. If your aptitude scores are strong and you also want to attempt GenC Next in a later window, add DSA-heavy coding practice (arrays, recursion, OOP concepts) before that specific drive opens — the written test for that track is materially harder.

faq.q: What is the difference between Cognizant GenC and GenC Next?
faq.a: GenC is the base fresher track where programming knowledge is recommended but not mandatory, tested through a 60–90 minute aptitude-heavy written round. GenC Next is for stronger coders and adds a two-part written test on conceptual code analysis and coding (DSA, OOP, databases), followed by a mandatory three-month internship before a higher, differential CTC is confirmed.

faq.q: Does GenC Pro still exist at Cognizant in 2026?
faq.a: Track naming is inconsistent across sources for the current cycle. Some prep sites reference a specialist track (PEGA, Salesforce, SAP, cybersecurity) called GenC Pro; others describe an equivalent track called GenC Elevate with a CTC close to base GenC rather than a large premium. This is genuinely unclear from public sources — verify the current track name and pay band on Cognizant's careers page for your specific drive.

faq.q: What CGPA is needed for Cognizant GenC?
faq.a: The consistently reported bar is 60% in Class 10, Class 12 and graduation, with no more than a one-year education gap after Class 12 and no pending backlogs at the time of selection. GenC Next doesn't have a separately confirmed CGPA cutoff, but written-test performance matters more there.

faq.q: What is the Cognizant GenC salary in 2026?
faq.a: GenC is widely reported around ₹4 LPA, with a monthly in-hand near ₹28,000–32,000. GenC Next is reported higher, in the ₹5.4–6.75 LPA range depending on the source, confirmed only after a mandatory three-month internship. These are reported figures from prep-site aggregations, not Cognizant's own published numbers.

faq.q: Is coding knowledge required for the Cognizant GenC interview?
faq.a: Not mandatory for the written test, which leans on aptitude — analytical reasoning, numerical and verbal skills. The technical interview still covers basic programming and DSA fundamentals regardless, so light coding revision is worth doing even if you're targeting GenC rather than GenC Next.

faq.q: How long is the Cognizant hiring process for freshers?
faq.a: Typically three stages: a written test, a technical interview, and an HR interview. GenC's process is generally quicker end-to-end than GenC Next's, which includes a longer two-part written round and, after selection, a mandatory three-month internship before the differential package is confirmed.

title: How Many Jobs Should I Apply to in India? A Real Number
h1: How Many Jobs Should I Apply to in India?
seo_title: How Many Jobs Should I Apply to? India Fresher Guide
seo_description: How many jobs should I apply to as an Indian fresher? See realistic weekly targets by profile and build your own tracker today.
excerpt: There is no magic number, but there is a realistic range. Here is how many jobs Indian freshers and early-career candidates should actually be applying to each week, and why quality of targeting matters more than raw volume.
content_html:
If you are asking how many jobs should I apply to, the honest answer is: there is no single correct number, but there is a realistic range. Most Indian freshers doing an active off-campus search should be sending out 15-25 well-targeted applications a week, not 5 and not 100. Fewer than that and you are not generating enough interview volume to survive a low response rate. More than that and you are almost certainly submitting generic applications that get filtered by ATS software before a human ever opens them. The number matters less than the ratio: how many of those applications are actually matched to your resume, skills, and CTC expectations. A candidate who sends 15 targeted applications a week for six weeks (90 total) will usually get more interview calls than someone who mass-applies to 300 postings with the same unedited resume. This piece breaks down what a realistic weekly target looks like by experience level, and how to build a tracking system so you know if your numbers are actually working.

Why there is no single right answer

Career forums and LinkedIn posts often throw out numbers like "apply to 500 jobs" or "you need at least 100 applications before one callback." These numbers get repeated so often they start to sound like research, but most of them are not backed by any published study specific to India. What is measurable is response rate, and response rate depends heavily on three things: how closely your resume matches the job description, how competitive the role is, and whether you are applying through a portal, a referral, or a campus drive.

According to Naukri's JobSpeak report for June 2026, white-collar hiring in India grew 6% year-on-year, with fresher hiring specifically growing 8% YoY and AI/ML roles leading at 25% YoY growth. That is a genuinely favourable hiring environment compared to the previous two years, but it does not mean applications convert easily. Growth in postings does not equal a low bar for each individual applicant — it means more roles exist, not that each one gets fewer applicants competing for it.

The volume trap

The mistake most freshers make is treating job search as a numbers game where volume alone wins. On platforms like Naukri and LinkedIn, a single fresher-level opening at a large IT services company can draw thousands of applications within 48 hours. If your resume is not tuned to the specific job description and does not clear applicant tracking system screening, adding more untargeted applications on top of that pile does not meaningfully improve your odds. It just adds hours of low-value effort to your week.

A realistic weekly target by profile

The right number changes depending on where you are in your career and how you are applying. The table below is a practical range based on how Indian hiring actually works in 2026: campus drives function differently from off-campus applications, and referral-based applications behave differently from cold portal applications.

ProfileWeekly application targetWhy
Final-year student, campus placements active3-5 off-campus applicationsCampus drives are your primary channel; off-campus is a backup, not the main effort
Fresher, no campus offer, active off-campus search15-25Enough volume to offset a naturally low response rate without becoming untargeted
0-2 years experience, employed but searching8-12Limited search hours; referrals and LinkedIn outreach should carry more weight than raw applications
0-2 years experience, unemployed, urgent search20-30Time is available; this is the phase to combine portal applications with direct outreach and referrals
Targeting only Tier-1 product companies (Google, Microsoft, Amazon-scale)5-10, highly tailoredVolume is far less useful than a strong referral or a portfolio project matched to the role

What actually moves the response rate

Before increasing how many jobs you apply to, it is worth fixing what happens to each application after you hit submit. Three levers matter more than raw count.

Resume-to-JD match

Most large Indian employers, including TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and Cognizant, route fresher applications through an ATS before a recruiter sees them. A resume using generic language instead of the terms in the actual job description gets filtered regardless of how many times you apply. Fixing your resume format for ATS compatibility before scaling up your applications will do more for your response rate than doubling your weekly volume.

Application channel

Not all applications are equal. A referral into a company, or an application made within the first 24-48 hours of a posting going live, converts at a meaningfully higher rate than an application made to a posting that already has 2,000+ applicants. If you are only using one portal, you are working with a smaller, more saturated pool. Spreading effort across multiple channels, including the major Indian job portals, campus drives, and LinkedIn direct outreach to hiring managers, increases the odds without inflating your total count.

Speed and consistency

A steady weekly rhythm beats a single weekend of frantic applying followed by two weeks of nothing. Recruiters post fresher roles continuously through the year, and postings for high-volume roles at IT services companies get refreshed often. Building a repeatable weekly process, similar to the approach in applying to jobs faster without losing quality, keeps your pipeline full without each application taking 40 minutes.

The application-to-offer funnel: setting expectations

It helps to think in terms of a funnel rather than a single number. Roughly, for a reasonably well-targeted fresher application in the current India market:

  • Out of every 15-20 targeted applications, expect 2-4 recruiter screens or online tests.
  • Out of every 3-4 screens, expect 1 to progress to a technical or panel interview.
  • Out of every 3-5 interview processes, expect 1 offer.

These ratios are not a published statistic — they are a rough, commonly cited rule of thumb among placement cells and career counsellors, and your personal numbers will vary by role, sector, and how tailored your applications are. Treat them as a sanity check, not a guarantee. If your ratios are far worse than this after 4-6 weeks of consistent, targeted applications, the problem is almost never volume. It is usually resume targeting, the roles you are choosing, or your CTC expectations relative to the market.

Building a tracker so the number means something

A weekly application target is only useful if you can see whether it is converting. Set up a simple spreadsheet with these columns: company, role, date applied, channel (portal/referral/campus), status, and follow-up date. Review it every Sunday. If you have applied to 60+ roles over four weeks with zero screens, that is a signal to change your resume or your target roles, not to apply to another 60. If you are getting screens but no interviews, the gap is usually the online test or the recruiter call, not the resume.

When off-campus volume needs to go up

For students who miss out on on-campus placement offers, off-campus applications become the primary channel, and the weekly target should sit closer to 20-25 rather than the lighter 3-5 range used during active campus season. This is also the point where mentorship or a second pair of eyes on your resume and application strategy tends to matter most, since you are now competing in a much larger, unfiltered applicant pool instead of a college-specific shortlist.

A quick sanity check before you scale up

Before pushing your weekly number higher, ask three questions. Is your resume tailored to the specific role, not just your general profile? Are you applying within days of a posting going live, not weeks later? Are you tracking outcomes so you actually know your conversion rate? If the answer to any of these is no, fix that first. Raising your application count without fixing targeting just means more rejections at the same rate, faster.

Frequently asked questions

Is applying to 100 jobs a day too many?

Yes, for almost everyone. At that volume you cannot realistically tailor each resume or cover letter, and most of those applications will be filtered by ATS software before a recruiter sees them. A focused 15-25 a week, done consistently, tends to produce better outcomes than an unsustainable one-day burst of 100.

How many jobs should a fresher apply to before hearing back?

There is no fixed number that guarantees a response, since it depends on your resume quality, the role, and the market. As a working range, expect to need somewhere between 15 and 40 targeted applications before your first genuine screening call, based on commonly cited placement-cell and career-counsellor estimates rather than a single confirmed study.

Should I apply to jobs I am not fully qualified for?

Applying to roles one notch above your current experience is reasonable, especially for freshers, since job descriptions in India often list requirements more aggressively than what is actually enforced. Applying to roles that need 4-5 years of experience when you have zero is usually a waste of the application.

Does applying to more jobs hurt my chances at any single one?

No, applying to multiple companies does not hurt you at any individual employer — recruiters expect candidates to be applying elsewhere. What can hurt you is applying to multiple open roles at the exact same company with a mismatched resume for each, which can look careless.

How long should I keep applying before changing strategy?

Give a consistent, tailored approach about four to six weeks before concluding it is not working. If you have sent 60-100 genuinely targeted applications in that window with almost no screens, the fix is usually your resume, your target role level, or your CTC expectations, not simply more applications.

Do referrals reduce how many applications I need to send?

Yes, significantly. A referral typically moves your resume past the initial ATS and recruiter-screening stage that filters out most cold applications, so a smaller number of referred applications can outperform a much larger number of cold ones.
