title: Salary Slip Components Explained: Every Line Item Decoded
h1: Salary Slip Components Explained: What Every Line on Your Payslip Means
seo_title: Salary Slip Components Explained for Indian Employees
seo_description: Salary slip components explained line by line — Basic, HRA, PF, PT and TDS — with a worked ₹8 LPA example. Read your payslip in five minutes.
excerpt: A line-by-line breakdown of Basic, HRA, DA, PF, professional tax and TDS on an Indian payslip, with a full worked example on an ₹8 LPA CTC.
content_html:
Your salary slip has roughly a dozen line items and most freshers only ever look at one number: what actually lands in the bank account. That's a mistake, because salary slip components are exactly what your recruiter is quoting when they say "8 LPA CTC" — and the gap between that number and your monthly credit is made up of Basic, HRA, DA, special allowance, and deductions like PF, professional tax and TDS. Once you can read each line, you can spot a lowball offer, check whether your employer is calculating PF correctly, and file your taxes without guessing. This article breaks down every component you'll see on an Indian payslip, in the order it usually appears, with a full worked example on a ₹8,00,000 CTC.

Why the Salary Slip Looks Nothing Like Your CTC Letter

The CTC (Cost to Company) figure in your offer letter is what the company spends on you in a year, including things that never touch your bank account — the employer's PF contribution, gratuity provisioning, and sometimes insurance premiums. Your salary slip only shows what's paid to you that month and what's deducted from that. That's why a ₹8 LPA offer rarely means ₹66,667 a month in hand; it's usually closer to ₹55,000–₹58,000 once PF, professional tax and any TDS are taken out. If you want the full mechanics of that gap, see our CTC vs in-hand salary breakdown.

The Earnings Side: What Makes Up Your Gross Salary

Gross salary is the sum of every earning component before any deduction. On most Indian payslips, it's split into four to six lines.

Basic Salary

Basic is the anchor figure — usually 35–50% of CTC at most Indian companies — because HRA, PF and gratuity are all calculated as a percentage of Basic (plus DA, where applicable). A lower Basic reduces your PF deduction and increases take-home pay in the short term, but it also reduces the PF corpus and gratuity you build over time. This is a deliberate structuring choice by the employer, not a random number.

House Rent Allowance (HRA)

HRA is meant to offset rent. It's commonly set at 40–50% of Basic (50% for metro cities like Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru and Chennai under the old tax regime's exemption rules; 40% for non-metros). If you pay rent and file under the old regime, a portion of HRA can be tax-exempt based on the lower of: actual HRA received, rent paid minus 10% of Basic+DA, or 50%/40% of Basic+DA. Under the new regime, HRA exemption isn't available at all — it's simply taxed as regular income.

Dearness Allowance (DA)

DA is standard for government and PSU employees, revised twice a year against inflation, but rare in private-sector payslips. If you work for a private company, you'll usually see a "special allowance" line instead of DA.

Special Allowance

This is the balancing figure — whatever is left of the fixed CTC once Basic, HRA and other named allowances are set. It's fully taxable, has no exemptions, and companies use it to round out the offer to the exact CTC number they quoted you.

Other Allowances

Depending on the company, you may also see Leave Travel Allowance (LTA, tax-exempt for two trips in a four-year block on actual travel bills under the old regime), conveyance allowance, and a food or meal allowance. These are usually small (₹1,000–₹3,000/month each) and mostly disappear if you've opted for the new tax regime, since most exemptions apply only under the old one.

The Deductions Side: What Comes Out Before You Get Paid

This is the side freshers skip past, and it's the side that matters most for your actual take-home number.

Provident Fund (EPF)

Both you and your employer contribute 12% of Basic+DA to EPF, but the calculation is capped: EPFO applies the statutory wage ceiling of ₹15,000 for the employer's contribution to the pension component (EPS) by default, though most companies now contribute 12% on actual Basic if it exceeds ₹15,000, per EPFO practice and employer policy. Your own 12% is a straight deduction from your salary slip. We've broken this down component-by-component, including the EPS split, in our PF deduction explainer.

Professional Tax (PT)

This is a small state-level tax, not a central one, so it varies by state and doesn't apply everywhere. Maharashtra, for instance, charges male employees earning above ₹10,000/month a flat ₹200/month (₹300 in February), while employees earning ₹7,500–₹10,000 pay ₹175/month; women are exempt up to ₹25,000/month in Maharashtra. Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, West Bengal and Gujarat have their own separate slabs. If your state doesn't levy professional tax at all — Delhi, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh don't — this line simply won't appear.

TDS (Income Tax Deducted at Source)

If your annual income puts you above the exemption threshold, your employer deducts income tax monthly and deposits it against your PAN, adjusted at the end of the year when you file your return. Whether this line shows up — and how large it is — depends on which tax regime you're under and how you've structured your salary. We cover the current slabs and the actual math in our new vs old tax regime comparison. Tax rules change with every Union Budget, so always check the current slabs on the Income Tax Department's e-filing portal before assuming last year's numbers still apply — the figures here are general information, not personalised financial advice.

ESI (Employees' State Insurance)

If your gross monthly wage is ₹21,000 or below, ESI is mandatory: 0.75% comes out of your salary and 3.25% is paid by the employer, funding subsidised medical care. Most salaried freshers with a package above ₹2.5 LPA won't see this line, since it phases out above the ₹21,000/month gross threshold.

A Full Worked Example: ₹8,00,000 CTC, Line by Line

Here's how an ₹8,00,000 CTC offer for a fresher in a non-metro city, on the new tax regime, typically breaks down on the payslip. Actual numbers vary by company structuring, but the proportions are realistic.

ComponentAnnual (₹)Monthly (₹)
Basic Salary (45% of CTC)3,60,00030,000
House Rent Allowance (40% of Basic)1,44,00012,000
Special Allowance (balancing figure)1,64,88013,740
Employer's EPF contribution43,2003,600
Gratuity provisioning17,3201,443
Statutory bonus / other70,6005,883
Gross CTC8,00,00066,667
Less: Employee EPF (12% of Basic)43,2003,600
Less: Professional Tax (non-Maharashtra flat example)2,400200
Less: TDS (new regime, income under ₹12L rebate)00
Net take-home (approx.)6,54,48054,540

Notice that the "Gross CTC" of ₹8,00,000 includes items — the employer's EPF share, gratuity provisioning, and a chunk of the statutory bonus — that never appear on a monthly credit slip. The employee actually sees a gross monthly salary of around ₹55,740 (Basic + HRA + special allowance), and after their own EPF and professional tax, lands at roughly ₹54,540/month. TDS shows as zero here because, under the new regime with the ₹75,000 standard deduction and the Section 87A rebate, taxable income after deductions stays under ₹12,00,000 annually for many freshers — but this depends entirely on your exact salary structure and any other income, so don't assume it applies to you without checking. To model your own number instead of this example, use the in-hand salary calculator.

How to Actually Use This Before You Sign an Offer

Three checks take less than five minutes and save you from a bad surprise on your first payday.

  • Ask for the CTC breakup in writing before you accept, not after — HR should give you a component-wise annexure, and a company that won't share one is a mild red flag.
  • Check the Basic-to-CTC ratio. A very low Basic (under 30% of CTC) inflates your headline number but shrinks your PF corpus and gratuity, both of which compound over years.
  • Recalculate the in-hand number yourself instead of trusting a recruiter's verbal estimate — the small deductions (PT, ESI, TDS) add up differently depending on your city and tax regime choice.

Common Mistakes Freshers Make Reading Their First Payslip

The most frequent one is comparing CTC across two offers as if it's the same as take-home pay — a ₹9 LPA offer with a bloated variable-pay component can pay less in hand each month than an ₹8 LPA offer with a straightforward fixed structure. The second is ignoring the professional tax and ESI lines entirely, then being confused when the in-hand number is a few hundred rupees short of a back-of-envelope calculation. The third is not checking whether PF is being deducted correctly at all — some smaller companies, especially those with under 20 employees, aren't registered with EPFO and skip it altogether, which is worth flagging before you accept an offer if long-term savings matter to you. If you're also deciding what number to quote a recruiter in the first place, our guide to answering the expected CTC question covers that separately.

Salary Slip Components at a Glance

Line ItemSideTypical Basis
Basic SalaryEarning35–50% of CTC
HRAEarning40–50% of Basic
DAEarningGovt/PSU only, revised biannually
Special AllowanceEarningBalancing figure
LTA / ConveyanceEarningFixed small amount, old regime only
Employee EPFDeduction12% of Basic+DA
Professional TaxDeductionState slab, where applicable
TDSDeductionBased on annual taxable income and regime
ESIDeduction0.75% if gross ≤ ₹21,000/month

None of this replaces reading your own payslip closely once you have one — every employer structures CTC slightly differently, and the exact percentages above are illustrative, not universal. But knowing what each line is supposed to represent means you'll notice immediately if something looks off.

What to Do If a Deduction Looks Wrong

If a line item on your payslip doesn't match what you expected — say, PF is missing entirely, or professional tax is being deducted in a state that doesn't levy it — raise it with HR or payroll directly and ask for the calculation logic in writing before assuming it's an error or letting it slide. EPF, in particular, is a legal entitlement once your employer crosses 20 employees, and quietly not being enrolled means you're losing employer-matched retirement savings every month without knowing it. Keep at least three to six months of payslips saved (most HR portals let you download PDFs), since you'll need them for rent agreements, loan applications, visa paperwork, and reconciling your Form 16 at tax-filing time. A salary slip is also the first document most background-verification agencies ask for when you switch jobs, so accuracy on it matters well beyond your monthly budgeting.

faq.q: What are the main salary slip components in India?
faq.a: The main salary slip components split into earnings — Basic Salary, HRA, DA (mostly government/PSU), and Special Allowance — and deductions — Employee EPF, Professional Tax (state-dependent), TDS, and ESI (if gross monthly wage is ₹21,000 or below). Together the earnings side adds up to gross salary, and gross minus deductions gives your net or in-hand salary.

faq.q: Why is my in-hand salary lower than the CTC I was offered?
faq.a: CTC includes costs that never reach your bank account, such as the employer's EPF contribution and gratuity provisioning, plus your own deductions like employee EPF, professional tax and TDS. A ₹8 LPA CTC commonly works out to roughly ₹54,000–₹58,000 in hand per month depending on your city, tax regime and company structure.

faq.q: Is professional tax deducted in every state?
faq.a: No. Professional tax is levied by state governments, not the centre, so it varies by state and some states — including Delhi, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh — don't levy it at all. In Maharashtra, for example, male employees earning above ₹10,000/month pay a flat ₹200/month (₹300 in February).

faq.q: What's the difference between Basic Salary and Gross Salary?
faq.a: Basic Salary is one component, usually 35–50% of CTC, used as the base for calculating HRA, EPF and gratuity. Gross Salary is the total of all earning components — Basic, HRA, DA, Special Allowance and any other allowances — before any deductions are applied.

faq.q: Does everyone have TDS deducted from their salary slip?
faq.a: No. TDS only applies once your estimated annual taxable income crosses the exemption threshold for your chosen tax regime. Many freshers on lower CTCs see a zero-TDS payslip most of the year. Tax slabs and rebate limits change with each Union Budget, so check current Income Tax Department guidance rather than relying on a previous year's figures.

faq.q: Why does my payslip not show a DA component?
faq.a: Dearness Allowance is standard for government and public-sector employees because it's revised twice a year against inflation indices. Most private-sector companies fold that adjustment into a 'Special Allowance' line instead, so DA simply won't appear on a typical private payslip.

title: How to Tailor Resume to Job Description in 20 Minutes
h1: How to Tailor Resume to Job Description in 20 Minutes
seo_title: How to Tailor Resume to Job Description Fast
seo_description: Tailor resume to job description with this repeatable 20-minute process, even at 30 applications a week. Start applying the steps today.
excerpt: A step-by-step, repeatable process to tailor your resume to a job description in about 20 minutes — plus what to never change, and how to keep tailoring even when you're applying to 30 roles a week.
content_html:
To tailor resume to job description requirements, you don't rewrite the whole document from scratch — you run the same 20-minute pass every time: pull the JD's top five requirements, match your existing bullets against them, rewrite your headline and summary, reorder your skills, then run a final formatting check. You keep your job titles, dates, and core achievements untouched. If you're applying to five or fewer roles a week, do this in full for every application. If you're applying to 30, you tailor a master resume in modular blocks instead of rewriting each one from zero. Here's the exact process, what to leave alone, a worked example, and how to scale it.

What tailoring actually means (and what it doesn't)

Tailoring isn't writing a new resume for every job — that's neither sustainable nor necessary. It's re-prioritising and re-wording the resume you already have so the first thing an ATS parser and a human recruiter see is the overlap between what you've done and what this specific role needs. A Harvard Business School study, reported by Jobscan, found that 88% of employers believe their own hiring systems filter out qualified candidates who don't precisely match the job description's language. That's the entire justification for tailoring: not to trick a system, but to stop your resume from looking like a mismatch to a filter that's doing exactly what it was built to do.

The 20-minute tailoring process, step by step

Minutes 0–5: Extract the JD's real requirements

Read the JD once for content, ignoring your resume entirely. Note the 5 requirements that appear as "must-have," repeat more than once, or sit in the first two lines of the role summary. For an off-campus drive JD from a company like Wipro or Cognizant advertising a ₹3.6–4.5 LPA fresher role, this is usually a mix of one or two tools, one soft skill, and the degree/branch requirement.

Minutes 5–12: Match your bullets to the top 5 requirements

Go bullet by bullet through your experience or project section. For each of the 5 requirements, find the bullet that already covers it — most freshers have the underlying experience, it's just not phrased to surface it. Move that bullet higher in the list if it isn't already near the top, and rewrite its first few words so the requirement's language appears early, not buried at the end of the sentence.

Minutes 12–17: Rewrite the summary and reorder skills

Your 2–3 line summary or headline should mention the role title and your top 2 matched requirements by name. In your skills section, move the tools this JD asks for to the top of the list — recruiters and quick human scans read top to bottom, and an ATS keyword match doesn't care about order, but a human skimming for 6–10 seconds does.

Minutes 17–20: Final ATS and formatting check

Save as a PDF (unless the application explicitly asks for .docx), confirm no tables or text boxes were introduced that could break parsing, and rename the file properly — a resume attached as "Resume(3).pdf" undoes minutes of good tailoring the moment a recruiter opens their downloads folder.

What NOT to change every time

Tailoring has a boundary, and crossing it is worse than not tailoring at all:

  • Your job titles and employment dates. Never reword a title to sound closer to the target role — recruiters cross-check this against your LinkedIn and any background verification, and a mismatch reads as dishonesty, not enthusiasm.
  • Your core achievements and numbers. The substance of what you did doesn't change; only which achievements you lead with and how you phrase the framing around them changes.
  • Your contact details, education section content, and overall structure. Constant structural changes increase the risk of formatting errors and give you nothing in return — an ATS doesn't reward a different layout, only better content overlap.

How to tailor when you're applying to 30 roles a week

Build a master resume with modular blocks

Keep one master document with every bullet you've ever written for every project, internship, and achievement — more content than fits on one page. For each application, you're not writing new bullets, you're selecting and lightly rewording from a bank you've already built. This turns a 20-minute-from-scratch process into a 6–8 minute selection-and-swap process once the bank exists.

Use a swap-in skills section

Maintain 3–4 versions of your skills section for the 3–4 role types you're actually applying to (say, Data Analyst, Business Analyst, and general Ops Analyst roles off Naukri). Swap the whole block in rather than editing skill-by-skill each time.

When to stop tailoring and just apply

Not every application deserves the full 20 minutes. If a JD is a near-duplicate of one you tailored for in the last 48 hours — same title, same 2–3 tools, same seniority — reuse that version with only the company name and 1–2 specifics changed. Save full tailoring passes for roles that materially differ from your last one, or that you're genuinely more interested in. Trying to give all 30 applications equal depth is how people burn out and start sending typo-riddled resumes by application 25 — see why resumes actually get rejected for what that costs you.

A worked example: tailoring one JD in the 20 minutes

The JD

Software Engineer Trainee — Pune. Strong fundamentals in Java or Python and data structures. Exposure to REST APIs and basic SQL. Work closely with senior engineers to debug and ship features. B.E./B.Tech, 2026 batch. ₹4–6 LPA.

Before tailoring

Summary: "Recent B.Tech graduate looking for a software engineering role to grow my technical skills." Skills section, in this order: Communication, C++, MySQL, Java, Teamwork, Python, Git.

After tailoring (5 minutes of work)

Summary: "B.Tech CSE graduate with Java and Python fundamentals, data structures coursework, and a project consuming REST APIs backed by SQL." Skills section reordered to: Java, Python, Data Structures, REST APIs, SQL, Git, Communication.

Nothing about the candidate's actual background changed — the same skills existed before and after. What changed is which of them lead, and whether the JD's own terms (Java, Python, REST APIs, SQL) appear in the first two lines a recruiter reads instead of buried behind "Communication" and "Teamwork," which say nothing this specific JD is screening for.

A tailoring checklist: change this, keep this

Resume elementChange per application?Why
Summary/headlineYes, every timeShould name the role and top matched requirement
Skills orderYes, every timeJD-relevant tools should sit at the top
Bullet order within a sectionYes, every timeMost relevant achievement leads, not buried third
Bullet wording (light edits)Yes, when it improves keyword overlapMirror the JD's exact terms where accurate
Job titles, dates, degreeNeverMust match verifiable records exactly
Core numbers/achievementsNeverSubstance shouldn't change, only framing

Common tailoring mistakes that aren't "changing too much"

Most tailoring mistakes aren't about overreach — they're about doing it unevenly. Rewriting the summary but forgetting to reorder the skills section leaves your strongest signal (the summary) pointing one way and your skills list pointing another, which reads as inconsistent rather than targeted. Tailoring late at night after 15 other applications and leaving a previous company's name inside a sentence you copy-pasted is the other common failure — always do the 3-minute final check specifically to catch leftover text from the last JD you tailored for, not just formatting. Neither mistake means you should tailor less; it means the last step of the 20-minute process — the final check — isn't optional even when you're moving fast.

Why this matters more at high application volume, not less

The instinct when you're applying to 30 roles a week is to stop tailoring because there's no time. That's backwards. At high volume, an untailored resume gets filtered out by the same generic-match problem 30 times instead of once — you're multiplying a fixable mistake, not avoiding it. If you're not sure how many applications a week is actually reasonable before this becomes about volume over quality, see how many jobs you should actually apply to, and if manual tailoring at that scale is genuinely eating your week, look at what auto-apply tools can and can't do for you before assuming you have to choose between speed and quality. Either way, the process above is what closes the gap between "I applied" and "I got a callback" — see also how to apply to jobs faster without cutting corners that cost you interviews.

faq.q: How long should it take to tailor a resume to a job description?
faq.a: About 20 minutes once you know the process: 5 minutes to extract the JD's top requirements, 7 minutes to match and reorder your bullets, 5 minutes to rewrite your summary and skills order, and 3 minutes for a final formatting check.

faq.q: What should I never change when tailoring a resume to a job description?
faq.a: Your job titles, employment dates, degree details, and the core substance of your achievements. These need to match your verifiable records and shouldn't shift between applications — only their order and framing should.

faq.q: How do I tailor my resume if I'm applying to 30 jobs a week?
faq.a: Build one master resume containing every bullet you've written, then select and lightly reword from that bank for each application instead of writing from scratch. Maintain 3–4 pre-built skills sections for the role types you actually apply to and swap the whole block in.

faq.q: Does tailoring a resume to a job description actually help with ATS?
faq.a: Yes. Research cited by Jobscan found that a large majority of employers believe their hiring systems filter out qualified candidates whose resumes don't closely match the job description's specific wording, which is exactly what tailoring corrects.

faq.q: Is it dishonest to tailor a resume for every job?
faq.a: No, as long as you're reordering and rewording real experience, not inventing it. Tailoring becomes a problem only when it crosses into changing job titles, dates, or claiming skills and outcomes you don't actually have.

title: Amazon India Interview Questions for Freshers: SDE-1 Rounds & CTC (2026)
h1: Amazon India Interview Questions: The Full SDE-1 Hiring Process
seo_title: Amazon India Interview Questions: SDE-1 Guide 2026
seo_description: Real amazon india interview questions for the OA, technical rounds and Bar Raiser, plus 2026 SDE-1 CTC bands. Start prepping your STAR stories now.
excerpt: A round-by-round breakdown of Amazon India's SDE-1 fresher hiring process, including the Bar Raiser round and Leadership Principles, with real example questions and 2026 CTC bands.
content_html:
Amazon India's fresher hiring for Software Development Engineer (SDE-1) roles runs six stages: resume screening, a long proctored online assessment with debugging and coding problems, two technical interviews on data structures and algorithms, a Bar Raiser round with an interviewer from outside your hiring team who holds veto power, and a final HR/hiring-manager conversation. Every single one of those rounds — not just a dedicated "behavioral" slot — also probes Amazon's 16 Leadership Principles. If you're preparing for amazon india interview questions, the thing that trips up most freshers isn't the DSA (which is genuinely hard but well-documented), it's underestimating how much weight the Leadership Principles carry in every round, including the coding ones. This guide covers the process, real example questions per round, and reported CTC bands for 2026.

Amazon India's fresher SDE hiring process at a glance

Amazon recruits fresh graduates (B.E./B.Tech/M.Tech/MCA/M.Sc in CS, IT or allied branches, typically with 60%+ marks or a 6.5+ CGPA and no active backlogs at joining) mainly into the SDE-1 role. According to a breakdown by MyInternships.in, the 2026 process runs across six stages:

StageFormatWhat it screens for
Resume screeningAmazon Jobs portal / campus driveAcademic eligibility, relevant coursework and projects
Online Assessment~3 hours, proctoredDebugging (6–8 questions), 2 coding problems, CS aptitude MCQs, work-style/work-simulation assessment
Technical Interview 145–60 minDSA problem-solving, project discussion, one or two Leadership Principles
Technical Interview 245–60 minAdvanced DSA, core CS fundamentals, Leadership Principles
Bar Raiser45–60 minCross-team calibration — technical depth plus Leadership Principles, with veto power over the offer
HR / Hiring Manager20–40 minLeadership fit, availability, offer discussion

Round 1: the Online Assessment

This is a long, proctored test — reportedly around three hours — combining several distinct sections rather than a single coding test.

What's actually in it

  • Debugging questions (6–8): you're given broken code and asked to identify and fix the bug, testing whether you can read unfamiliar code under time pressure, not just write your own from scratch.
  • Two coding problems: typically array/string manipulation, hashing, or basic graph/tree problems solvable in 20–30 minutes each at a fresher level — for example, "find all pairs in an array that sum to a target value" or "check if a binary tree is balanced."
  • CS fundamentals MCQs: OS, DBMS, networking and OOP basics.
  • Work-style / work-simulation assessment: scenario-based questions describing a workplace situation (e.g., a teammate missing a deadline, conflicting priorities from two stakeholders) and asking you to rank possible responses. This section is effectively an early, automated pass at Leadership Principles — answers that reflect Ownership and Customer Obsession score better than ones that simply avoid conflict.

Rounds 2 and 3: the technical interviews

Two back-to-back technical rounds, each 45–60 minutes, blend DSA problem-solving with Leadership Principles questions rather than separating them.

Example DSA questions

  • "Given a string, find the longest substring without repeating characters." A strong answer starts by stating the brute-force complexity (O(n²) or O(n³)) out loud, then moves to a sliding-window approach with a hashmap tracking last-seen indices to get O(n), and talks through the two-pointer logic as they code.
  • "Given a binary tree, print its level-order traversal." Good candidates immediately reach for a queue-based BFS and clarify edge cases (empty tree, single node) before writing code.
  • "Design a data structure that supports insert, delete, and getRandom in O(1) average time." This is a step up in difficulty from the OA and tests whether you can combine a hashmap with a dynamic array — interviewers are watching whether you ask clarifying questions before diving in, not just whether you eventually get the right structure.

Example Leadership Principle questions woven into the same rounds

  • "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision on a team project. What did you do?" (Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit) — a good answer describes the specific disagreement, how you raised it with evidence rather than just opinion, and what happened once a decision was made, including whether you committed to it even if it wasn't your preferred outcome.
  • "Describe a time you went beyond what was expected of you in a project or internship." (Ownership) — strong answers include a measurable outcome (time saved, bug prevented, users affected), not just an adjective like "I worked really hard."
  • "Tell me about the most difficult bug you've debugged." (Dive Deep) — interviewers want the specific steps you took to isolate the root cause, not just "I eventually fixed it."

Amazon's own guidance and multiple prep resources (e.g. Exponent, IGotAnOffer) consistently recommend preparing 6–8 STAR stories in advance, each mapped to two or three Leadership Principles, with specific, quantified outcomes rather than vague claims.

Round 4: the Bar Raiser

The Bar Raiser is Amazon's most distinctive round and the one freshers are least prepared for because it isn't documented as clearly outside the company. The interviewer is deliberately drawn from a completely different team, has no stake in filling your specific role, and is specifically trained to check whether you'd raise Amazon's overall hiring bar — not just whether you're good enough for one team's immediate need. Crucially, the Bar Raiser has the authority to veto a hire even if every other interviewer wants to move forward.

What actually happens in this round

Expect a mix of a moderately hard DSA problem and deep behavioral probing — the Bar Raiser often re-asks about a story you already told an earlier interviewer, specifically to check for consistency and depth. If your "Dive Deep" story from Technical Interview 1 sounds different or shallower when the Bar Raiser asks a follow-up, that's a red flag they're specifically listening for. The fix is simple but often skipped: know your own stories cold enough that you can answer follow-up questions three levels deep, not just recite a rehearsed two-minute version once.

Round 5: HR / hiring manager

The final round covers availability, relocation, and overall leadership fit, and is also where compensation and offer logistics get discussed. It's shorter and lower-stakes than the technical and Bar Raiser rounds, but a poor fit signal here (evasiveness about availability, disinterest in the role) can still stall an otherwise strong loop.

CTC and pay bands reported for Amazon India SDE-1 freshers in 2026

Amazon does not publish a single official fresher CTC figure, and reported numbers vary by source, role and whether the hire is through campus or lateral/off-campus channels. Treat the following as reported ranges rather than confirmed company disclosures:

  • Base salary: reported around ₹17–22 LPA for SDE-1.
  • Sign-on bonus: reported around ₹2–6 LPA, typically paid across the first one to two years rather than upfront in full.
  • RSUs (stock): reported around ₹6–12 LPA face value at grant, vesting over four years on a back-loaded schedule (commonly cited as roughly 5% / 15% / 40% / 40% across the four years), meaning your actual Year-1 and Year-2 realized compensation runs meaningfully below the headline total.
  • Total CTC: commonly reported in the ₹28–34 LPA range for SDE-1, though this figure blends base, sign-on and stock face value in a way that overstates what you'll actually see in your bank account in year one — don't plan your finances around the headline number.

Because the RSU vesting schedule is back-loaded, it's worth working through CTC vs in-hand salary and thinking specifically about early-career cash flow before accepting, rather than anchoring purely on the total package figure recruiters quote.

A worked example: answering a Leadership Principles question with real depth

Question: "Tell me about a time you had to make a decision without all the information you wanted." A weak answer: "During my internship, I had to build a feature without complete requirements, so I made some assumptions and built it anyway." That's vague and has no outcome.

A strong answer: "During my final internship sprint, my mentor was on leave and I needed to decide whether our export feature should support CSV only or also Excel, with no one available to confirm the requirement. I looked at the three most recent support tickets referencing exports, saw two explicitly asked for Excel, and decided to build both formats behind a feature flag so I could ship CSV on time and add Excel without a redeploy. It shipped on schedule, and when my mentor returned, she confirmed Excel was in fact the higher-priority one 60% of our target users needed." This answer shows real judgment (using available data instead of guessing blindly), a concrete decision, and a verifiable outcome — exactly the structure Amazon interviewers are trained to probe for under principles like Ownership and Customer Obsession.

How to prepare given the time you have

If you have a month: build a bank of 40–50 solved DSA problems across arrays, strings, trees, graphs and dynamic programming, and separately draft 6–8 STAR stories mapped to specific Leadership Principles with quantified outcomes. If you have a week: prioritise the STAR stories (they're reusable across every round including the OA's work-simulation section) and do timed practice on medium-difficulty problems rather than trying to cram new topics. Whatever your timeline, rehearse your resume walkthrough and practice answering "tell me about yourself" in a way that naturally sets up your strongest stories, and think through how to negotiate salary before the HR round given how back-loaded Amazon's RSU structure is.

The freshers who do best in Amazon India's process treat the DSA rounds and the Leadership Principles rounds as one interview, not two. An interviewer who sees you code cleanly and explain your reasoning with the same rigor you use for your STAR stories is exactly who the Bar Raiser is looking to pass.

faq.q: What is the Amazon India interview process for freshers?
faq.a: For SDE-1 roles it's typically six stages: resume screening, a roughly 3-hour proctored online assessment (debugging questions, two coding problems, CS MCQs, and a work-style/work-simulation section), two technical interviews on DSA, a Bar Raiser round, and a final HR/hiring-manager round. Leadership Principles are assessed in every round, not just one dedicated slot.

faq.q: What is a Bar Raiser interview at Amazon?
faq.a: It's a round conducted by an interviewer deliberately drawn from outside your hiring team, trained to evaluate whether you'd raise Amazon's overall hiring bar rather than just meet one team's immediate need. The Bar Raiser has veto power over the final hiring decision even if other interviewers want to proceed, and often re-probes stories you told earlier to check consistency.

faq.q: How many Leadership Principles should I prepare stories for?
faq.a: Most prep guides, including Exponent and IGotAnOffer, recommend preparing 6-8 STAR-format stories, each mapped to two or three of Amazon's 16 Leadership Principles, with specific and quantified outcomes rather than vague claims.

faq.q: What is the fresher CTC for Amazon India SDE-1 in 2026?
faq.a: Reported figures put base salary around ₹17-22 LPA, a sign-on bonus around ₹2-6 LPA paid over the first year or two, and RSUs around ₹6-12 LPA at grant vesting over four years on a back-loaded schedule. Total CTC is commonly reported around ₹28-34 LPA, though actual realized pay in year one is lower than that headline figure due to the vesting schedule.

faq.q: What kind of coding questions are asked in Amazon India's online assessment?
faq.a: The OA reportedly includes 6-8 debugging questions where you fix broken code, plus two original coding problems on topics like arrays, strings, hashing, or basic trees/graphs, alongside CS fundamentals MCQs and a work-style simulation section.

faq.q: Do Amazon India's technical interview rounds ask behavioral questions too?
faq.a: Yes. Amazon's Leadership Principles are woven into every round including the technical ones, not confined to a single HR interview. Expect a DSA problem followed by one or two behavioral questions in the same 45-60 minute slot.

title: How to Explain an Employment Gap on Your Resume and in Interviews
h1: How to Explain an Employment Gap Without Sounding Defensive
seo_title: How to Explain an Employment Gap in India
seo_description: Learn how to explain an employment gap with word-for-word answers for exam prep, illness, layoffs and backlogs. Write your own answer today.
excerpt: An employment gap is common for Indian freshers preparing for UPSC, CAT or GATE, recovering from illness, or hit by a layoff. Here is what to write on the resume, what to say out loud, and word-for-word answers for the five most common situations.
content_html:
An employment gap is not the disqualifier most Indian freshers think it is. Recruiters at TCS, Infosys, Wipro and mid-size firms see gaps on resumes every single day — exam preparation for UPSC, CAT or GATE, a family medical emergency, a startup that shut down, a layoff, or backlogs that pushed a degree by a year. What actually costs you the offer is not the gap itself. It is a vague, defensive, or dishonest explanation of it. This guide gives you word-for-word answers for the five gaps Indian candidates face most often, and tells you exactly what belongs on the resume versus what you say out loud in the interview.

Why an employment gap worries Indian recruiters less than you think

Hiring in India has been unusually volatile since 2023. According to layoff-tracking reports covering 2026, Indian tech firms and their global counterparts have cut over a lakh jobs this year alone, with TCS alone affecting close to 19,000–24,000 employees in its own restructuring and Oracle cutting roughly 12,000 roles in India as part of a global 30,000-person reduction. When gaps caused by layoffs are this common across an entire hiring cycle, an interviewer who penalises every gap on principle is penalising a large share of the candidate pool. Most experienced interviewers know this and have adjusted their questioning accordingly — they are checking how you handled the gap, not whether one exists.

That said, a gap you cannot explain clearly still reads as a red flag. The goal is not to hide it. The goal is to have a explanation ready that is short, factual, and shows what you did with the time.

What goes on the resume versus what you say out loud

These are two different documents with two different jobs. The resume needs to survive an ATS scan and a six-second human skim. The interview conversation needs to survive follow-up questions. Treat them differently.

On the resume

  • Use years, not months, for older gaps (2022–2024) so a short scan does not look like six empty months when it was closer to eleven.
  • Add one line under the gap period if it is over six months — for example "UPSC Civil Services preparation, 2023–2024" or "Caregiver, family medical leave, 2023." One line is enough. Do not write a paragraph.
  • If you did anything income-generating or skill-building during the gap — freelance work, an online certification, a part-time role — list it as its own line, even if it was unpaid or informal.
  • Never leave a gap unlabeled and unexplained if it is longer than four to five months. An unlabeled gap invites the interviewer to assume the worst.

In the interview

  • Say it in one or two sentences, then move immediately to what you learned or how you are different now.
  • Do not apologise for the gap or over-explain. A long, nervous answer signals insecurity more than the gap itself does.
  • Never volunteer more detail than asked, especially around medical or family situations. "A family health situation that needed my presence" is a complete, professional answer. You are not obligated to share a diagnosis.

Word-for-word answers for the five most common Indian employment gaps

Use these as a starting structure, not a script to memorise verbatim — adjust the specifics to your real situation, because interviewers can tell a rehearsed line from a lived one.

1. Exam preparation — UPSC, CAT, GATE or similar

Resume line: "Civil Services (UPSC) examination preparation, 2023–2025."

What to say: "After graduating, I spent close to two years preparing for the UPSC exams. I didn't clear the final list, and I made the decision this year to move into industry instead of attempting again. That preparation is actually useful here — I spent two years reading current affairs, economics and policy analysis daily, which built the kind of structured reading and long-form writing habit that most fresh graduates haven't had to build. I'm applying that same discipline to [role/skill] now."

This works for CAT and GATE preparation too — swap the specifics. For CAT, mention the quant and logical reasoning practice; for GATE, mention the depth of core-subject revision. The key move is the same: state the fact plainly, own the outcome without self-flagellation, and connect the skill built during prep to something the employer cares about.

2. Family illness or caregiving

Resume line: "Family caregiving responsibilities, Jan 2024–Mar 2025."

What to say: "My [family member] had a serious health issue during that period and I was the primary support at home. That responsibility has eased now, and I'm able to commit fully to a full-time role. I kept my technical skills current by [specific: an online course, freelance project, volunteering] during that time."

You do not need to name the illness or the family member's condition. "A serious health issue" and "primary support" are sufficient. If an interviewer pushes for more detail than that, it is a fair, polite boundary to say you'd rather focus on your readiness to work now.

3. A startup that failed or shut down

Resume line: keep the role listed normally with an end date, and optionally note "company ceased operations" only if directly asked.

What to say: "I joined a seed-stage startup as one of the first ten hires. We ran for about fourteen months before the founders shut it down when the next funding round didn't close — that happens to a large share of early-stage startups in India, it wasn't performance-related on my end. In that time I ended up owning [specific, concrete responsibility] because the team was so small, which gave me exposure I wouldn't have had this early at a larger company."

Startup shutdowns are common enough in the Indian ecosystem that most interviewers will not read this as a personal failure, provided you can speak concretely about what you actually did there. Vague answers ("it just didn't work out") are what make interviewers suspicious, not the shutdown itself.

4. A layoff

Resume line: keep the role and dates as they were; no note needed on the resume itself.

What to say: "My role was eliminated in a company-wide restructuring in [month/year] — it wasn't specific to my performance, and my manager can confirm that if useful. Since then I've been focused on [specific activity: interviewing, upskilling, a short project] and I'm looking for a role where I can [specific goal tied to the job]."

Offer a reference check proactively if you were laid off, not fired for cause — it signals you have nothing to hide. If the layoff was large and well-known (a big-tech or large-IT-services round), you can even name it briefly: "I was part of the [company] layoffs in [year]" carries less stigma than an unnamed, vague gap, because the interviewer likely read about it already.

5. Academic backlogs that delayed graduation

Resume line: list your actual graduation year; do not list an expected year that didn't happen. If asked directly why the timeline is longer than four years, be ready with the answer below.

What to say: "I had two backlog papers in my third year that pushed my final graduation by one year. I cleared both and graduated with [CGPA/percentage]. It taught me to manage my course load more realistically, and I haven't had that issue since."

Do not over-apologise for backlogs. Indian engineering colleges fail large numbers of students in specific papers most years, and recruiters at IT services firms who hire in bulk from tier-2 and tier-3 colleges have seen this pattern often enough that a calm, factual answer lands better than a defensive one. What actually damages you here is dishonesty on the graduation year, not the backlog itself — if it's checked against your degree certificate later and doesn't match, that becomes a much bigger problem than the original gap.

A quick reference: gap type, resume treatment, spoken answer length

Gap typeWhat to write on resumeIdeal spoken answer length
Exam prep (UPSC/CAT/GATE)One line naming the exam and years3–4 sentences
Family illness/caregiving"Family caregiving responsibilities" + dates2–3 sentences, no medical detail
Startup shutdownNormal role entry with end date3–4 sentences with one concrete achievement
LayoffNo special note needed2–3 sentences, offer reference check
Academic backlogActual graduation year, not expected year2 sentences, factual, no apology

Mistakes that turn a manageable gap into a red flag

  • Changing dates to hide a gap. Recruiters cross-check resume dates against offer letters and background verification. A caught inconsistency is far worse than the original gap.
  • Over-explaining in the interview. A ninety-second answer to a question that needed twenty seconds reads as anxiety, even when the underlying reason is completely reasonable.
  • Leaving the gap completely unaddressed on the resume and hoping it's not noticed. Most interviewers who read resumes carefully will ask about it anyway, and being caught off-guard is worse than having a ready answer.
  • Framing the gap only around what happened to you, with no mention of what you did. Even a small activity — a free online course, tutoring, volunteering — gives the interviewer something forward-looking to hold on to.

How this fits into the rest of your application

An employment gap is one detail among many an interviewer is weighing. It matters far less than how you answer tell me about yourself or the standard HR interview questions that follow it. If your resume is otherwise strong and you have a calm, specific answer ready, most Indian recruiters — particularly at high-volume IT services hiring, where thousands of freshers are processed every quarter — will move past the gap in under a minute and get back to assessing your actual skills. Spend more of your prep time on why resumes get rejected in the first screening round; a gap rarely causes that rejection on its own.

Building the gap into your broader job search

If your gap is still ongoing — you're preparing for an exam now, or recently laid off — the smartest move is to shorten it wherever practical. Freelance work, contract projects, or even structured volunteering give you both an income bridge and a legitimate line to add to your resume. If you're returning to the job market after a long gap, look specifically at how to get a job as a fresher guidance rather than generic experienced-hire advice, since the expectations, screening questions and resume format differ meaningfully between the two tracks.

faq.q: How long of an employment gap is considered a problem in India?
faq.a: Gaps under three to four months rarely draw questions. Beyond six months, most Indian recruiters will ask directly, so have a one- or two-sentence answer ready. The length matters less than whether your explanation is clear and consistent with your resume dates.

faq.q: Should I mention my employment gap in my cover letter?
faq.a: Only if the gap is recent and likely to be the first thing a reader notices, and even then, one sentence is enough. For most candidates it's better handled in the interview than in a cover letter, where space is limited and better spent on why you fit the role.

faq.q: Is it okay to say I was preparing for UPSC if I didn't clear it?
faq.a: Yes. State it plainly, mention you've decided to move into industry, and pivot immediately to a skill or habit the preparation built. Interviewers are far more concerned with vague or evasive answers than with an unsuccessful attempt at a genuinely difficult exam.

faq.q: What if I was fired, not laid off in a restructuring?
faq.a: Be honest but brief, and focus on what you changed afterward rather than relitigating the situation. If you were let go for a specific, fixable reason, naming the lesson you took from it is more convincing than denying or minimising what happened.

faq.q: Do employment gaps affect background verification in India?
faq.a: Background verification agencies used by large Indian employers typically confirm employment dates, not the reason for a gap between jobs. What they will flag is a mismatch between your stated dates and your previous employer's records, which is why accuracy matters more than framing.

faq.q: Can I just leave a short gap off my resume entirely?
faq.a: For gaps under two to three months, using only years (rather than months) on your resume is standard practice and not considered dishonest. For longer gaps, omitting them entirely is riskier than addressing them briefly, since an unexplained multi-month blank is more noticeable than a one-line explanation.

title: 6 LPA In Hand Salary: The Real Month-by-Month Take-Home
h1: 6 LPA In Hand Salary: What You Actually Take Home Every Month
seo_title: 6 LPA In Hand Salary: Full Monthly Breakdown for 2026
seo_description: See the exact 6 LPA in hand salary after PF, gratuity, professional tax and income tax for FY 2026-27, with the full breakdown. Calculate your own number now.
excerpt: A full month-by-month breakdown of what a ₹6,00,000 CTC actually pays out after PF, gratuity, professional tax and income tax, with a comparison of 40% vs 50% basic pay.
content_html:
For a ₹6,00,000 CTC in India, the in-hand salary works out to roughly ₹42,000 to ₹44,000 a month if your employer calculates provident fund on your full basic. Where PF is capped at the statutory ₹15,000 wage ceiling instead — which is the more common arrangement — the same offer pays closer to ₹45,000 a month after the standard deductions — provident fund, gratuity, professional tax and income tax. The exact 6 LPA in hand salary you get depends mostly on how your employer splits the CTC between basic pay and allowances, not on the tax slab, because taxable income at this level usually falls inside the tax-free zone created by the Section 87A rebate for FY 2026-27. A ₹6 LPA offer with a 40% basic will hand you slightly more cash every month than the identical CTC structured with a 50% basic, because a higher basic pulls a bigger share into employer PF and gratuity — both real money, just money you don't see monthly. Here is the exact month-by-month math, with both basic ratios worked out.

CTC vs in-hand salary: why 6 LPA never means ₹50,000 a month

A CTC (cost-to-company) figure like ₹6,00,000 a year is not what lands in your bank account divided by twelve. It is the total annual cost the employer books against you: basic pay, allowances, its own contribution to your provident fund, a gratuity provision, and sometimes insurance premiums. Some of that money is cash you receive every month. Some of it, like employer PF and gratuity, is money the company sets aside for your future, and you only see it when you withdraw your PF or complete five years and become eligible for gratuity. Understanding the difference between CTC and in-hand salary is the first step to reading any offer letter correctly, and it matters more at ₹6 LPA than at a higher CTC, because the fixed deductions form a bigger share of a smaller number.

The deductions between your CTC and your bank account

Every payslip in India removes roughly the same set of items from CTC before cash reaches you. Line by line:

  • Basic pay — the anchor figure. HR sets it as a fixed percentage of CTC, typically 35–50%. HRA, PF and gratuity are all calculated off this one number.
  • HRA (House Rent Allowance) — usually 40–50% of basic, paid monthly, and taxable unless you claim the rent exemption against it.
  • Employer PF contribution — 12% of basic, paid by the company into your EPF account. Of that 12%, 3.67% is credited to your EPF balance and 8.33% is diverted to the Employees' Pension Scheme (EPS). It sits inside your CTC but never touches your monthly salary account. Our breakdown of how PF deduction actually works covers the employee side of this in more detail.
  • Gratuity provision — roughly 4.81% of basic, the standard figure under the 15/26 formula in the Payment of Gratuity Act, set aside as a CTC line item but paid out only if you complete five years of continuous service with that employer. Our gratuity calculation guide walks through the exact formula.
  • Employee PF contribution — another 12% of basic, this time deducted from your own gross pay rather than added by the company. This is the PF line that actually shows up as a deduction on your payslip.
  • Professional tax — a small state-level tax, deducted monthly, ranging from ₹0 to ₹200 depending on where you're employed.
  • Income tax (TDS) — deducted monthly based on your projected annual taxable income and the regime you've declared to your employer.

Month-by-month math: ₹6,00,000 CTC with a 40% basic

Here is what a common 6 LPA structure looks like when basic pay is set at 40% of CTC — a ratio many mid-sized Indian employers use for entry-level offers.

ComponentAnnual (₹)Monthly (₹)
CTC6,00,00050,000
Basic pay (40% of CTC)2,40,00020,000
HRA (50% of basic)1,20,00010,000
Employer PF (12% of basic)28,8002,400
Gratuity provision (4.81% of basic)11,544962
Special allowance (balancing figure)1,99,65616,638
Gross monthly salary (before employee deductions)5,59,65646,638
Employee PF (12% of basic)28,8002,400
Professional tax (state-dependent example)2,400200
Income tax (TDS, new regime)00
Approximate in-hand salary~5,28,000~44,000

The income tax line reads zero because, under the FY 2026-27 slabs, taxable income after the ₹75,000 standard deduction comes to roughly ₹4.85 lakh — well inside the range the Section 87A rebate wipes out entirely for anyone with taxable income up to ₹12,00,000. That is the single biggest reason a 6 LPA in hand salary feels close to the gross figure once PF and professional tax are accounted for: there is effectively no income tax to worry about at this income level under the new regime.

What changes if basic is 50% instead of 40%

Some employers structure the same CTC with a higher basic, especially when they want the PF and gratuity numbers on the offer annexure to look more generous. Here is the same ₹6,00,000 CTC with basic at 50%.

ComponentAnnual (₹)Monthly (₹)
Basic pay (50% of CTC)3,00,00025,000
HRA (50% of basic)1,50,00012,500
Employer PF (12% of basic)36,0003,000
Gratuity provision (4.81% of basic)14,4301,203
Gross monthly salary (before employee deductions)5,49,57045,798
Employee PF (12% of basic)36,0003,000
Professional tax (example)2,400200
Approximate in-hand salary~5,11,000~42,600

Income tax stays at zero in both versions — the 87A rebate covers you either way at this CTC. The difference of roughly ₹1,400 a month, about ₹17,000 a year, comes entirely from a bigger basic pushing more money into employer PF and gratuity, neither of which you receive monthly. A higher basic isn't a bad deal — it means a bigger PF corpus and a bigger eventual gratuity payout — but if someone tells you a higher-basic 6 LPA offer will put more cash in your account each month, the math says otherwise.

Variable pay and other CTC add-ons that can shift the number further

The two tables above assume a clean, fully-fixed ₹6,00,000 CTC. In practice, a fair number of 6 LPA offers in India — especially from BPOs, sales-heavy roles and some IT services companies — carve out 10–20% of the CTC as variable pay tied to a monthly, quarterly or annual performance rating rather than paying it as fixed salary. If your offer letter shows ₹6,00,000 CTC with, say, 90% fixed and 10% variable, your guaranteed monthly in-hand drops by roughly that 10% until the variable component is actually paid out, and it may not be paid in full if targets aren't met. Read the annexure specifically for the words "variable pay," "performance bonus" or "incentive," not just the headline CTC number.

A second add-on to watch for is group health/term insurance. Many companies bundle a group mediclaim premium into the CTC as a fixed cost, which behaves like employer PF and gratuity — it's real value, but it never appears as cash in your account. A smaller number of companies deduct a portion of the premium from the employee's own gross pay instead, which would show up as one more line item reducing your in-hand number below the ₹42,000–₹44,000 range worked out above. If your offer letter has a line for "insurance" or "GMC" under deductions rather than under company contributions, ask HR which side it sits on before you sign.

Income tax on a 6 LPA salary: FY 2026-27 slabs and the 87A rebate

Union Budget 2026 made no change to the income tax slabs, so the FY 2026-27 new-regime rates remain the same as the previous year:

Taxable income slabRate (new regime)
Up to ₹4,00,000Nil
₹4,00,001 – ₹8,00,0005%
₹8,00,001 – ₹12,00,00010%
₹12,00,001 – ₹16,00,00015%
₹16,00,001 – ₹20,00,00020%
₹20,00,001 – ₹24,00,00025%
Above ₹24,00,00030%

Salaried employees also get a flat ₹75,000 standard deduction, and Section 87A gives a rebate of up to ₹60,000 to anyone with taxable income up to ₹12,00,000 — which is what makes tax effectively nil for a ₹6 LPA salary in the new regime. Weigh this against the old tax regime before assuming the new regime is automatically better for you; if you carry a home loan or heavy Section 80C investments, the comparison can shift, though for most people drawing their first or second salary at this CTC, the new regime — also the default unless you opt out — leaves more in hand.

Professional tax by state — the part people forget

Professional tax is a small monthly state-level deduction that quick online calculators often skip, and it's one reason two people on identical 6 LPA offers in different cities see slightly different in-hand numbers.

StateThresholdMonthly tax
MaharashtraAbove ₹10,000/month (men); ₹25,000/month (women)₹200 (₹300 in February)
Karnataka₹25,000/month and above₹200 flat
Gujarat₹12,000/month and above₹200
West BengalAbove ₹40,000/month₹200 (lower slabs from ₹110)
Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, RajasthanNot applicableNo professional tax

At a monthly gross of roughly ₹45,000–₹47,000 for a 6 LPA offer, most professional-tax states will deduct ₹200 a month from you. It's a small number, but it's one more reason a generic "6 LPA in hand salary" figure from a random online tool can be off by a few hundred rupees from your actual payslip.

How to check your own number

The fastest way to stop estimating and see your real figure is to run your own CTC breakup — basic percentage, HRA, and your state — through Cheatcode's in-hand salary calculator. If your offer letter already lists basic, HRA and PF separately in the annexure (most do), plug in those exact numbers rather than assuming a 40% or 50% basic split. That assumption is the only thing that ever moves the answer by more than a few hundred rupees at this CTC, since income tax is usually zero either way.

One honest caveat: tax slabs, rebate limits and PF rules are set, and occasionally changed, at every Union Budget. The FY 2026-27 numbers above reflect what was in force as of August 2026. Treat this article as information to help you read your own payslip, not as financial advice — verify the current rules before making a decision that hinges on the exact rupee figure.

faq.q: What is the in-hand salary for a 6 LPA CTC in India?
faq.a: Roughly ₹42,000 to ₹44,000 a month, depending mainly on how much of the CTC is basic pay and which state you're employed in. Income tax is usually zero at this level under the FY 2026-27 new tax regime.

faq.q: Is any income tax deducted from a 6 LPA salary?
faq.a: Under the new regime, almost never. Taxable income after the ₹75,000 standard deduction stays well below ₹12,00,000, so the Section 87A rebate cancels the small tax the slabs would otherwise charge. Under the old regime, without deductions like 80C or HRA exemption, a small TDS is possible.

faq.q: Does a higher basic salary always mean higher in-hand pay?
faq.a: No, usually the opposite. A higher basic increases employer PF and gratuity, both of which are locked away rather than paid monthly, and also increases your own PF deduction. In-hand pay tends to be slightly lower with a higher basic, even though your retirement corpus grows faster.

faq.q: Why do two people with the same 6 LPA CTC get different take-home pay?
faq.a: The two most common reasons are the basic-to-CTC ratio their specific employer uses, and the professional tax rate in the state they're employed in, which ranges from ₹0 to ₹200 a month depending on the state.

faq.q: Does gratuity actually reduce my monthly salary?
faq.a: It reduces the cash portion of your CTC that's paid out monthly, but it isn't lost. It becomes a lump sum payable if you complete five years of continuous service with that employer, under the Payment of Gratuity Act.

faq.q: Will this 6 LPA in-hand salary figure still be accurate next year?
faq.a: Only if the tax slabs, standard deduction and PF rules don't change. All three are set in the Union Budget and have moved in recent years, so re-check the current numbers before relying on the exact figure.

title: Cover Letter for Internship: A Full Worked Example
h1: How to Write a Cover Letter for Internship Applications (Full Example)
seo_title: Cover Letter for Internship: Full Example + 3 Variations
seo_description: A full worked cover letter for internship applicants with no experience, plus what changes for research, startup and mass-hiring roles. Start writing yours.
excerpt: A full worked example of a cover letter for an internship for a student with no experience, plus what changes for a research internship, a startup, and a mass-hiring program like TCS's.
content_html:
A good cover letter for internship applications has one job: convince someone that a student with little or no work history is worth an interview anyway. That means it can't lean on the "five years of experience in X" opening that generic templates suggest — it has to substitute coursework, projects, competition results, or plain self-taught effort for the experience section a full-time cover letter would use. The core structure stays the same across every internship: who you are, why this specific team, one or two concrete proof points, and a clear ask. What changes is the proof points and the tone, and they shift noticeably between a research internship, a startup internship, and a mass-hiring program like TCS's or Infosys's annual intake. Below is a full worked example, followed by exactly what to change for each of those three situations.

What a cover letter for an internship needs to do differently

Drop any line that apologizes for not having experience — "I know I don't have much experience, but..." tells the reader to lower their expectations before they've even reached your proof points. Replace it with the strongest evidence you actually have: a project, a competition placement, a piece of self-directed learning, or a relevant piece of coursework, described specifically enough that it reads as real rather than generic. Keep the whole letter to around 250–300 words. For the mechanics of structure and formatting that apply to any cover letter, our general guide on how to write a cover letter is worth reading alongside this one; what follows here is specific to the internship context.

A second difference is the ask itself. A full-time cover letter usually implies "hire me for this role"; an internship cover letter is often implicitly asking for something smaller and more specific — a chance to learn under a particular team, for a fixed and known duration. Naming that duration and your availability clearly (semester dates, exam schedule, how many hours a week you can commit if it's part-time alongside college) removes a scheduling question the reader would otherwise have to ask you separately, and shows you've thought about the practical shape of the internship rather than just the title.

Full worked example: a cover letter for a student with no experience

This is written for a third-year computer science student applying to a data analytics internship at a mid-size company, with no prior internship, using project work and self-taught skills as the proof points.

Subject: Application for Data Analytics Intern — [Your Name], [College Name], Third Year

Dear [Hiring Manager's name],

I'm a third-year B.Tech Computer Science student at [College name], and I'm applying for the Data Analytics Intern role posted on [portal name]. I haven't had a formal internship yet, but three things make me a strong fit for this specific role.

First, I built a dashboard tracking placement statistics for my college's training and placement cell using Python and Power BI, cleaning and merging four years of inconsistent spreadsheet data into something the faculty team actually uses today. Second, I placed in the top 15 of [a named hackathon or competition] by building a churn-prediction model on a retail dataset — the kind of problem your job description lists under core responsibilities. Third, I've spent the last two semesters teaching myself SQL and data visualization outside of coursework, specifically because I wanted to work on real business data rather than classroom exercises.

I'd like the chance to bring that same curiosity to [Company name]'s team for the [duration] internship. I'm available to start from [date] and can commit full-time for the internship's full duration. My resume and a link to the placement dashboard project are attached below.

Thank you for considering my application.

[Your name]

[Phone] | [Email] | [LinkedIn or portfolio link]

Notice what carries the letter: three specific, checkable claims, each tied to a real artifact (a dashboard, a competition ranking, a self-taught skill applied to a real problem), not adjectives like "hardworking" or "passionate about data." That pattern — specific claim, named artifact, tie-back to the job description — is what changes across the three variations below, while the overall shape of the letter stays the same.

What changes for a research internship

A research internship — whether it's a lab placement, a professor-led project, or a structured programme like the Summer Research Fellowship Programme jointly run by the Indian Academy of Sciences, INSA and NASI for undergraduates — expects an academic register, not a business one. Name the specific area of research and, if you can find it, the specific paper, dataset or ongoing project the lab is known for, rather than describing the department in general terms. Mention the exact coursework or lab technique that's relevant (a named method, software, or instrument, not "strong academic background"), and state clearly that you can commit to the full research duration, which for programmes like SRFP typically runs eight to ten weeks over a summer. Drop any language about salary or stipend negotiation entirely — these programmes almost always have a fixed, published stipend, and raising it reads as misjudging the context.

What changes for a startup internship

Startups rarely have a formal hiring pipeline for interns, so the cover letter is often the only screening document a founder or a small team actually reads before a call. The tone can be more direct and less formal than a corporate letter — naming the specific product, a feature you've used, or a piece of the company's public work (a blog post, a demo, an open-source repo) shows you did more than skim the "About" page. Startups value speed and initiative more than polish, so a shorter letter that gets to the point in the first two lines works better than a fuller, more formal structure. Be explicit about your availability and how quickly you can start, since a small team often needs to fill a gap immediately rather than plan around a fixed onboarding calendar the way a larger company would.

It's also worth naming something small and specific you noticed while using or researching the product — a bug, a feature you wished existed, an unusual design choice — because it signals genuine curiosity rather than a mass-sent application. Many startup internships are found through college WhatsApp groups, Internshala, or a founder's own LinkedIn post rather than a formal jobs page, so the same letter often needs to work as a cold email too; keep a version that opens with why you're reaching out to them specifically, in case there's no formal "Dear Hiring Manager" to address it to at all.

What changes for a mass-hiring internship program

Programs like TCS's annual internship intake or Infosys's InfyTQ-linked hiring run through an application portal and an ATS rather than a human reading individual emails one by one — a TCS internship, for context, typically pays a stipend in the ₹2–2.8 lakh per annum range depending on the role and location, and runs on fixed application windows for a defined batch of students. Whatever text box the application calls a "cover letter" or "statement of purpose" is far more likely to be scanned for keyword overlap with the job description than read as a piece of writing, so match the language of the posting closely and keep sentences short and specific rather than narrative. This is the one situation where an ATS-aware approach to your resume and cover letter genuinely outranks a more creative, story-driven version — save the personality for the interview round, if there is one, and use the written application to get through the filter.

Internship typeToneEmphasize
Research (lab, SRFP-style programme)Academic, specificNamed research area, relevant coursework or method, full-duration availability
StartupDirect, informalSpecific product knowledge, speed, availability to start immediately
Mass-hiring program (TCS, Infosys-style)Keyword-matched, conciseExact terms from the job posting, ATS-friendly structure over narrative
General/unclear processThe worked example aboveSpecific projects, named artifacts, clear availability

Common mistakes that get internship cover letters ignored

  • Opening with "Dear Sir/Madam" when the hiring manager's name is findable. A minute on LinkedIn or the company's team page usually finds a name; using it signals you did that minute of work.
  • Restating the resume line by line. The cover letter should add context the resume can't — why this team, why now, what a bullet point actually involved — not repeat it.
  • Apologizing for lack of experience. Every internship applicant has limited experience; the letter's job is to make the experience you do have sound specific, not to pre-apologize for what you don't have.
  • Leaving out availability and duration. Many internships have a fixed window; not stating when you can start and for how long forces the reader to guess or, more likely, move to the next application.
  • Writing more than a page. For an internship application, 250–300 words is enough; longer letters for an entry-level, low-experience application read as padding rather than substance.
  • Getting the company or portal's name wrong from reusing a template. If you're applying to several internships listed on Internshala or similar portals, always re-check the company name, role title and one detail before sending — a copy-paste error is an instant filter-out for many recruiters.

Whichever version you write, keep two things constant: use the standard cover letter format so it's easy to skim, and check it against a couple of real cover letter examples before sending, particularly if this is your first one. The format is forgiving; specificity is not — it's the one thing every version above depends on.

If you're sending the application as an email rather than uploading a document to a portal, the same content works, but check that your subject line and the first two lines still make sense on their own before anyone opens the attachment — a recruiter or founder skimming a crowded inbox often decides whether to open a message based on those two things alone. Whichever internship you're applying to, the letter is doing its job if a reader who knows nothing about you finishes it with one clear, specific reason to move you to the next round, rather than a vague, positive impression they can't quite pin down.

faq.q: Do I need a cover letter for an internship if I have no experience?
faq.a: Yes, if the application allows one — it's your best chance to substitute projects, coursework and self-taught skills for the work experience you don't have yet. Skipping it means relying entirely on a resume that, for a student, often has little to differentiate it from hundreds of others.

faq.q: How long should an internship cover letter be?
faq.a: Around 250 to 300 words. Long enough to make two or three specific, concrete points, short enough that a recruiter or hiring manager reads the whole thing rather than skimming it.

faq.q: What should I write instead of work experience?
faq.a: Specific projects, competition or hackathon results, self-taught skills applied to a real problem, or relevant coursework — described with enough detail (tools used, what you built, what changed) that it reads as real rather than generic.

faq.q: Should I email the cover letter directly to a startup founder?
faq.a: If you can find their email or LinkedIn and the posting doesn't specify an application process, yes — a short, direct note referencing something specific about their product often works better than a formal application form for early-stage startups.

faq.q: Do mass-hiring programs like TCS's internship even read individual cover letters?
faq.a: Rarely as a human-read document at the first stage. These run through an application portal and ATS, so keyword overlap with the job description matters more than narrative writing. Match the posting's language closely.

faq.q: Can I use the same cover letter for every internship I apply to?
faq.a: Keep the core structure and your strongest proof points constant, but change the company name, the specific reason you want that team, and which proof point you lead with based on what the posting emphasises. A cover letter that's obviously identical across applications is easy for a reader to spot.
